About me

I am a Lead Data Modeler and BI Leader with 11 years of experience. Data modeling is my core craft: I design conceptual, logical and physical models in ERwin and ER/Studio, and build dimensional, Data Vault 2.0 and canonical models that turn business questions into trusted, governed data. Around that core I deliver BI with Qlik Sense and NPrinting, ETL and CDC pipelines, and Qlik Replicate streaming with L3 support, RCA and incident management on AWS, Snowflake and Linux. I also work as a business analyst and product owner (SAFe POPM certified): running requirement workshops with senior stakeholders, writing BRD/FRD, epics and user stories, owning the backlog and Agile delivery in Jira through UAT and release. I lead and mentor teams of 2 to 7 and report progress, risks and decisions to steering and executive forums.

  • Data modeling, end to end: conceptual models agreed with the business, logical models in ERwin and ER/Studio, and physical designs tuned for Snowflake, Databricks Delta Lake, Oracle and SQL Server, with DDL, keys, constraints and clustering handed to developers.
  • Every style, one platform: Kimball dimensional models with explicit grain and SCD handling, Data Vault 2.0 (hubs, links, satellites, hash keys), canonical models, semantic layers (Denodo) and ontology concepts, and Medallion layering (Bronze, Silver, Gold).

Knowledge · Data modeling

Data modeling

32 blocks on data modeling, from the basics to enterprise architecture, using a bank as the running example. Tap a block to open it.

Part 1 · Foundations

Picture a bank with 1 million customers, 1.5 million accounts, 3 million cards and hundreds of millions of transactions. The CFO asks: "Which customers hold a savings account, a credit card and an active loan, and how much revenue did they generate last quarter?"

The bank cannot answer reliably if the same customer is stored differently in each system, if nobody has defined how customers relate to accounts, or if old values were overwritten. Data modeling is the discipline of organizing business information so that meaning, relationships and integrity are preserved, and the structure fits the workload it serves.

The vocabulary

TermPlain meaningBank example
EntityA thing the business cares about (a noun)Customer, Account, Card, Transaction
AttributeA fact that describes an entityCustomer name, account number, balance
RelationshipHow two entities connect (a verb)Customer holds Account
RecordOne real instance of an entityCustomer C101, Ravi
DomainThe values an attribute may takeAccount status: Active, Dormant, Closed
Primary keyWhat makes each row uniqueCustomer_ID
Foreign keyA column that points to another table's keyAccount.Customer_ID
ConstraintA rule the database enforcesAccount number must be unique
Business ruleThe policy behind a constraintA minor cannot open a current account alone
GrainWhat exactly one row representsOne transaction; one account per day
MetadataData about dataColumn definition, owner, sensitivity
SchemaThe full structure of tables, columns, keys and relationshipsThe bank's CUSTOMER, ACCOUNT, TRANSACTION design

Finding entities from a business story

Requirement: "A customer can open several accounts. Each account can have many transactions. Joint accounts are allowed."

StepWhat to doResult
1. Underline the nounsCandidate entitiesCustomer, Account, Transaction
2. Underline the verbsCandidate relationshipsopens, has, joint-holds
3. Note the rulesCardinality and constraintsMany accounts per customer; joint ownership possible; a transaction belongs to one account

Easy way to remember: an entity is a noun, an attribute is an adjective that describes it, and a relationship is the verb that connects two nouns.

Requirements come first

A model is only as good as the questions it was built to answer. Before drawing anything, sit with the business and agree on the following.

Ask aboutWhy it mattersOutput
Decisions they makeReveals the metrics and dimensions neededBusiness questions and KPIs
Terms they argue aboutExposes undefined words such as 'active customer'Agreed glossary definitions
Reports they trust todayGives a reconciliation targetAcceptance criteria (e.g. matches Finance within 0.1%)
Volume, latency, retention, securityShapes architecture as much as entities doNon-functional requirements

Traceability: nothing in the model is orphaned

Business requirement→Conceptual entity→Logical attribute→Physical column→Report or KPI

Keep a traceability matrix so any column can be defended ("it exists because Risk needs delinquency by branch") and any change can be impact-assessed.

Grain: the most important decision in analytical design

Grain answers one question: what exactly does one row represent? Take customer Ravi, who has two accounts and five transactions.

TableGrain (one row =)Rows
Transactions: T101…T105 with amountsOne transaction5
Account totals: A100 = ₹1,700, A200 = ₹1,000One account for the period2
Customer total: Ravi = ₹2,700One customer for the period1

The business activity is identical; only the level of detail changes. Mixing grains in one table is the classic cause of wrong numbers.

Why grain matters: fan-out

Account A100 has a balance of ₹50,000 and three transactions. Joining the balance to the transactions repeats ₹50,000 three times, so summing gives ₹1,50,000, which is wrong. The fix is to aggregate first, report at one common grain, or keep balances in their own snapshot table.

Rule: before designing any fact table, finish the sentence “One row in this table represents exactly ____.” If the team cannot, the design is not ready.

Like building a house: the owner's brief (what rooms do I need), the architect's blueprint (how rooms connect and their sizes), and the construction drawing (which materials, wiring and plumbing). Data models follow the same three steps.

Conceptual

What exists? Business entities and how they relate, in business words, for stakeholders.

Customer — holds — Account — records — Transaction

Logical

How is it organized? Attributes, keys, cardinality and optionality, normalized, independent of any database product.

CUSTOMER(customer_id, name)
ACCOUNT(account_id, type)
ACCOUNT_HOLDER(customer_id, account_id, role)

Physical

How is it stored? Data types, constraints, indexes, partitioning, clustering and DDL for the chosen platform.

customer_id BIGINT
amount NUMBER(18,2)
CLUSTER BY (txn_date)

Same bank, three levels

AspectConceptualLogicalPhysical
FocusBusiness meaningDetailed structureImplementation
EntitiesYesYesTables
AttributesFew or noneAll, with definitionsColumns
KeysNot shownPrimary, foreign, alternateEnforced or informational
Joint ownership'Customer holds Account' (many-to-many)Resolved with ACCOUNT_HOLDERTable with composite key and foreign keys

Physical model sample (illustrative)

CREATE TABLE customer (
  customer_id  BIGINT       PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  date_of_birth DATE
);
CREATE TABLE account (
  account_id   BIGINT       PRIMARY KEY,
  account_type VARCHAR(30)  NOT NULL,
  open_date    DATE
);
CREATE TABLE account_holder (
  customer_id    BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customer(customer_id),
  account_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES account(account_id),
  ownership_role VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, account_id)
);

How the tools help

ERwin and ER/Studio keep definitions, naming standards, versions and traceability across all three levels. Forward engineering generates DDL from the model. Reverse engineering rebuilds a model from an existing database. Complete compare finds drift between the model and the live database. Reverse engineering recovers structure, not business meaning, so definitions must still be reviewed with the business.

An entity-relationship (ER) diagram draws entities as boxes and relationships as lines. The most common notation in banks and consultancies is Crow's Foot.

Symbol (Crow's Foot)Meaning
Single barExactly one (mandatory)
CircleZero (optional)
Fork (crow's foot)Many
Bar + forkOne or many (1..*)
Circle + forkZero or many (0..*)

Other notations: Chen (relationships as diamonds, common in teaching) and UML class diagrams (common in application design).

Core ideas

ConceptPlain explanationBank example
Strong entityExists on its ownCustomer
Weak entityCannot be identified without an owner; carries the owner's key plus a partial keyLoan Installment (Loan_ID + Installment_No)
Identifying relationshipThe owner's key becomes part of the weak entity's keyLoan owns its Installments
Total participationEvery instance must take partEvery account has at least one holder
Partial participationTaking part is optionalA customer may have no account yet
Recursive relationshipAn entity relates to itselfEmployee manages Employee; Account has Parent Account
Supertype / subtypeA general entity with specialized kindsAccount → Savings, Current, Loan

Implementing supertype and subtype

PatternHowBest when
One table for allSingle ACCOUNT table with a type column and nullable subtype columnsSubtypes are similar, queries span all of them
Table per subtypeSeparate SAVINGS, CURRENT, LOAN tablesSubtypes differ greatly and are queried separately
Super table plus subtype tablesACCOUNT holds common columns; subtype tables hold the rest, linked 1:1Common queries plus subtype-specific detail

Good habits: singular entity names, verbs on relationship lines, one diagram per subject area, and a definition for every entity and attribute.

Keys identify rows and connect tables. Take a CUSTOMER table with Customer_ID, PAN, Email and Name.

KeyMeaningBank example
Super keyAny column set that is unique (may contain extras)Customer_ID + Name
Candidate keyA minimal unique set (nothing can be removed)Customer_ID; PAN
Primary keyThe candidate chosen as the identifierCustomer_ID
Alternate keyA candidate not chosen as primaryPAN
Natural keyA real-world identifierAccount number
Business keyThe identifier the business uses within a source or domainCore-banking Customer_ID
Surrogate keyA meaningless number generated by the systemCustomer_SK = 1002
Hash keyA deterministic hash of the business key (Data Vault)Hash(source + customer id)
Composite keySeveral columns togetherCustomer_ID + Account_ID in ACCOUNT_HOLDER
Foreign keyA column that references another table's keyAccount.Branch_ID → Branch.Branch_ID
Unique keyEnforces uniqueness without being the primary keyRegistered email, if the rules require it
Partial keyIdentifies a weak entity within its ownerInstallment_No within a Loan

Surrogate versus business key

Ravi moves from Hyderabad to Mumbai. The warehouse keeps both versions of his record:

Customer_SKCustomer_ID (business key)CityCurrent
1001C101HyderabadN
1002C101MumbaiY

The business key says who the customer is; the surrogate key says which stored version. Facts point to the surrogate key so each transaction keeps the version that was true at the time.

Avoid: using a value that can change (name, phone, email) as a key. A surrogate key is unique within its own table; it is not automatically unique across systems.

Cardinality says how many instances of one entity can relate to instances of another.

One-to-one (1:1)

An account and its settings record. Implemented with a unique foreign key or a shared primary key. A separate table is justified only when lifecycle or security differs; otherwise one table is simpler.

One-to-many (1:M)

One branch manages many accounts; each account has one home branch. The foreign key sits on the many side (ACCOUNT.Branch_ID).

Many-to-many (M:N)

One customer can own several accounts, and one joint account can have several customers. Putting Customer_ID in ACCOUNT would allow only one customer per account, so the relationship needs its own table.

The many-to-many relationship still exists in the business; the bridge only represents it correctly. Sample rows:

customer_idaccount_idownership_rolevalid_from
C001A101Primary2024-01-01
C002A101Joint2024-01-01
C001A102Primary2025-03-10

How each modeling approach handles M:N

ApproachTechniqueSample structureWatch out for
3NF / OLTP / Inmon EDWAssociative (intersection) tableCUSTOMER_ACCOUNT(customer_id, account_id, role, valid_from)Define uniqueness and effective dates; joint ownership can start and end
Kimball dimensionalBridge table between fact/dimension and the multivalued dimension, often with a weighting factorBRIDGE_ACCOUNT_CUSTOMER(account_group_key, customer_key, weight)Without weights, a ₹10,000 balance is counted twice (once per holder)
Data VaultLink table that joins hubsLINK_CUSTOMER_ACCOUNT(link_hk, customer_hk, account_hk, load_dts, record_source) plus an effectivity satelliteLinks never remove M:N; they record every association ever seen
Graph databaseA relationship (edge) is a first-class object(Customer)-[:HOLDS {role}]->(Account)Edges carry attributes; no bridge table needed

Traps to know

TrapWhat happensFix
Fan trapJoining two independent 1:M paths multiplies rows and inflates totalsAggregate each path separately, then combine
Chasm trapAn optional path silently drops rowsUse outer joins or model the relationship explicitly
AllocationA joint balance belongs to two customers; do both get 100%?Agree a rule: split by weight, assign to primary holder, or count distinct accounts
Temporal ownershipJoint holders change over timeKeep effective dates on the bridge or link

Part 2 · Integrity and normalization

Constraints are rules the database enforces. Integrity is the outcome: data you can rely on.

TypeRuleExample
Entity integrityPrimary key is unique and not nullEvery customer row has a Customer_ID
Referential integrityA foreign key must match a parent row (or be null)An account cannot point to a branch that does not exist
Domain integrityValues stay within the allowed set or rangeStatus in (Active, Dormant, Closed); amount >= 0
Temporal integrityValidity periods do not overlap or leave gapsOne current address per customer
Business rulePolicy enforced in code or pipelinesOverdraft cannot exceed the approved limit
ConstraintWhat it does
NOT NULLValue is mandatory
UNIQUENo duplicates
PRIMARY KEYUnique and not null identifier
FOREIGN KEYLinks to a parent table
CHECKCustom condition on a column
DEFAULTValue used when none is supplied

Cascade rules

What happens to child rows when a parent is deleted: RESTRICT blocks the delete, CASCADE deletes children, SET NULL clears the reference. Banks usually restrict, then close or flag records instead of deleting them, to preserve audit trails.

Cloud warehouses: Snowflake and Redshift record primary and foreign keys but generally do not enforce them. Enforce integrity through pipeline tests, reconciliation and data quality rules, and document the keys anyway for tools and readers.

Normalization removes repeated facts so each fact is stored once. Consider this poorly designed table:

CustomerAccountBranchBranch_City
RaviA101B01Hyderabad
RaviA102B01Hyderabad
PriyaA103B02Mumbai

If branch B01 moves, several rows need updating and missing one creates inconsistency (update anomaly). Deleting the last account of a branch would erase the branch itself (deletion anomaly), and a new branch cannot be recorded until it has an account (insertion anomaly).

The idea behind every normal form is the functional dependency: if A determines B (Branch_ID → Branch_City), then B should be stored once, in a table keyed by A. A correct split is lossless: joining the pieces rebuilds the original exactly.

FormPlain-language ruleViolation exampleFix
1NFOne value per cell; no repeating groups; rows identifiablePhones = '9999, 8888'One row per phone in CUSTOMER_PHONE
2NFEvery non-key column depends on the whole keyACCOUNT_HOLDER(Customer_ID, Account_ID, Customer_Name): name depends only on Customer_IDMove Customer_Name to CUSTOMER
3NFNon-key columns depend on the key and nothing elseACCOUNT(Account_ID, Branch_ID, Branch_City)BRANCH(Branch_ID, Branch_City)
BCNFEvery determinant is a candidate keyA non-key column that decides part of the keySplit so each determinant becomes a key
4NFIndependent multi-valued facts are stored separatelyPhones and contact channels in one table create 4 rows for 2 phones × 2 channelsCUSTOMER_PHONE and CUSTOMER_CHANNEL
5NFNo join dependency beyond what keys implySupplier–product–branch rules that must be rebuilt by joining three tablesDecompose into binary relations
6NFIrreducible relations; one attribute per table plus timeAddress and risk status change on different datesOne history table per independently changing attribute

Result of the 3NF fix

ACCOUNT(account_id, branch_id)
BRANCH (branch_id, branch_city)

Memory aid for 3NF: every column describes the key, the whole key and nothing but the key. It is a reminder, not a replacement for the formal definition.

In practice: operational (OLTP) systems aim for 3NF or BCNF. 4NF to 6NF appear in specific cases, such as independent histories. Stop earlier when another split costs more than it protects.

Normalization protects writes: each fact lives in one place, so updates are safe. Denormalization serves reads: facts are combined or repeated so queries need fewer joins. Neither is "better"; they answer different workloads.

The same data, two ways

Normalized (OLTP)Denormalized (reporting)
CUSTOMER(customer_id, name)
ACCOUNT(account_id, customer_id, branch_id)
BRANCH(branch_id, city)
TRANSACTION(txn_id, account_id, amount)		TXN_REPORT(txn_id, amount, account_id, customer_name, branch_city)
A city change updates one BRANCH rowA city change must update every affected report row
Reading a transaction with customer and city needs 3 joinsReading it needs none
DimensionNormalizationDenormalization
Primary goalIntegrity, no redundancyFast, simple reads
Typical homeCore banking, OLTPReporting, analytics, marts
UpdatesLocal and safeMay touch many copies
JoinsUsually moreUsually fewer
StorageOften lowerOften higher
Main riskComplex, slower readsInconsistent copies
ExamplesCustomer, Account tablesCustomer account summary; star schema

Common denormalization techniques

TechniqueUse
Pre-joined or wide tableFewer joins for a dashboard
Copied descriptive columnAvoid a lookup on every query
Pre-aggregated tableRepeated totals such as monthly branch sales
Materialized viewDatabase maintains the summary
Dimensional (star) modelPlanned denormalization with clear grain

Do not assume denormalization is always faster. Columnar engines such as Snowflake and Redshift, with compression, clustering and caching, can make joins cheap. Measure before duplicating data. A star schema is intentionally denormalized, but not every wide table is a good dimensional model; grain and conformed dimensions still apply.

Rule of thumb: normalize where data is written, denormalize where data is read, and keep a documented path from one to the other (the ETL).

Part 3 · Warehouse design: Kimball, Inmon, Data Vault

FeatureOLTPOLAP
PurposeRun operationsAnalyze operations
ExampleTransfer ₹500 nowMonthly transfer trend by branch
QueriesShort, selective, by keyLarge scans and aggregations
DataCurrent stateHistory, integrated
DesignNormalized (3NF)Dimensional or integrated EDW
WorkloadMany concurrent writesRead-heavy
Example systemCore bankingEnterprise data warehouse

These are tendencies, not laws: OLTP tables are sometimes denormalized, and warehouses sometimes use normalized or vault models.

The layers in a data platform

LayerMeaningTypical content
Source / OLTPWhere data is createdCore banking, cards, CRM
Landing / stagingRaw copy of source dataFiles and tables as received
ODSIntegrated, near-current operational viewCustomer and account as of now
EDWIntegrated, historical, governed warehouse3NF or Data Vault
Data martSubject-specific slice for a teamCards mart, risk mart (star schemas)
LakehouseLake storage with warehouse-style tables (Delta, Iceberg)Raw to curated in one platform
Semantic layerGoverned business definitionsMetrics, joins, access rules

HTAP (hybrid transactional and analytical processing) lets one engine serve both workloads and reduces copies, but needs strict workload isolation so a month-end report never slows payments.

Take a bank statement. Each line tells you what happened (the amount); the date, account, branch and channel tell you the context. The measurable event is a fact; the context is a dimension. Dimensions answer who, what, where, when and how.

The four-step design process

StepQuestionBank example
1. Choose the business processWhat activity are we measuring?Card transactions
2. Declare the grainWhat does one row mean?One card transaction
3. Choose the dimensionsWhat context describes it?Date, customer, card, merchant, channel
4. Choose the factsWhat is measured?Amount, fee, count

Star schema

One central fact table surrounded by denormalized dimensions. Simple for BI tools and business users.

SchemaStructureStrengthCost
StarFact plus denormalized dimensionsFewest joins, easiest for BIRepeated descriptive values
Snowflake schemaDimensions normalized into sub-tables (Branch → City → State → Country)Less repetition in large hierarchiesMore joins, harder to navigate
Galaxy (constellation)Several facts sharing conformed dimensionsCross-process analysisNeeds strong governance of shared dimensions

Note: snowflake schema is a design pattern; Snowflake is a cloud data platform. They are unrelated.

Bus matrix: the enterprise plan

Rows are business processes; columns are conformed dimensions. A tick means the process uses that dimension. It tells the program which shared dimensions to build first.

Business processDateCustomerAccountBranchProduct
Card transactions✔✔✔✔
Loan disbursement✔✔✔✔✔
Deposit balances✔✔✔✔✔
Fraud alerts✔✔✔✔

Drill-across: query two facts separately at the same grain, then combine the answers on conformed dimensions. Never join two fact tables directly.

Fact typeQuestion it answersBank exampleGrain
TransactionWhat happened?Debit or credit postingOne posting
Periodic snapshotWhat was the state at each interval?Daily account balanceOne account per day
Accumulating snapshotHow far has a process progressed?Loan application lifecycleOne application
Factless (event)Did it happen?Customer attended an advisory sessionOne attendance
Factless (coverage)What was eligible?Customer eligible for a productOne customer-product interval
AggregateWhat is the precomputed summary?Monthly transactions by accountOne account per month

Additive, semi-additive and non-additive measures

Account A101 closes Monday at ₹10,000 and Tuesday at ₹12,000. Adding them gives ₹22,000, which is not the balance on any day.

TypeRuleExample
AdditiveCan be summed across every dimensionTransaction amount
Semi-additiveCan be summed across accounts at one date, never across datesClosing balance (use latest, average or period end over time)
Non-additiveNever summed; recompute from the partsInterest rate, default rate = defaults ÷ loans

Remember: transactions flow, balances stand, ratios must be recalculated. Distinct counts also do not add across groups, so pre-compute them or use approximate counts. Always state the grain to avoid double counting.

TypeMeaningBank exampleWhy use it
ConformedShared with identical meaning across factsDIM_CUSTOMER for cards and loansConsistent cross-product reporting
Role-playingOne dimension used in several rolesDIM_DATE as transaction, posting and settlement dateOne table, many meanings
DegenerateIdentifier kept in the fact, no dimension tableTransaction numberNo descriptive attributes to store
JunkGroups unrelated low-cardinality flagsIs_Online, Is_International, Is_Fraud_SuspectedKeeps the fact narrow
Mini-dimensionSplits rapidly changing attributesCustomer risk band and income bandAvoids huge SCD2 growth
OutriggerA dimension that references anotherCustomer → GeographyReuse a shared dimension
ShrunkenA subset of a larger dimensionMonth from DateAggregate-level reporting
InferredPlaceholder created before details arriveUnknown customer C105Handles early-arriving facts
MultivaluedSeveral members apply to one factSeveral beneficiaries on one accountNeeds a bridge table
HierarchicalLevels for roll-upBranch → Region → CountryDrill up and down
StaticRarely or never changesCurrency code, calendarNo history handling needed
Rapidly changingChanges oftenBehavioral segmentMove to a mini-dimension

Add an Unknown member (for example key −1) to every dimension so facts never lose their join when a reference is missing.

Conformed dimensions are the most important senior-level idea. Cards and loans must agree on what “Customer” means before Customer 360 reporting can be trusted. Conformance needs compatible meaning, keys, attributes and governance, not just two tables with the same name.

Story: Ravi lived in Hyderabad until 15 November and moved to Mumbai on 16 November. Should reports show where he lives now, where he lived at the time, or both? Each SCD type gives a different answer.

Type 0: retain the original

Never changed, even if the real world changes. Use for date of birth or original acquisition channel.

CustomerOriginal_City
RaviHyderabad

Type 1: overwrite

The old value is lost. Use for corrections or attributes where history has no value.

CustomerCity
RaviMumbai

Type 2: add a new row (full history)

SKCustomerCityValid_FromValid_ToCurrent
101RaviHyderabad1 Jan16 NovN
102RaviMumbai16 Nov9999-12-31Y

Use half-open intervals: valid_from <= event_date < valid_to, so versions never overlap. Facts keep the surrogate key of the version that was true. Use for address, segment, risk class and regulatory history.

Type 3: add a column (limited history)

CustomerPrevious_CityCurrent_City
RaviHyderabadMumbai

Keeps only one previous value. Use when the business needs just current and previous.

Type 4: separate history table

Current dimensionHistory table
Ravi, MumbaiRavi, Hyderabad, from 1 Jan
Ravi, Mumbai, from 16 Nov

Fast current lookups with history kept elsewhere.

Type 5: mini-dimension plus current pointer

Fast-changing attributes (risk band, income band) move to a mini-dimension. Facts reference the historical profile; the customer dimension also holds the current profile key.

DIM_CUSTOMER(customer_sk, customer_id, current_risk_profile_sk)
DIM_RISK_PROFILE(risk_profile_sk, risk_band, income_band)

Type 6: hybrid (1 + 2 + 3)

SKCustomerHistorical_CityCurrent_CityCurrent
101RaviHyderabadMumbaiN
102RaviMumbaiMumbaiY

Each version keeps its own city, while Current_City is overwritten on all versions so reports can use either view.

Type 7: dual access

The fact stores both the version key (what was true then) and the durable business key (what is true now). A current-view of the dimension gives Type 1 reporting, the versioned table gives Type 2.

Choosing a type

TypeHistory keptTechniqueUse when
0Original onlyNo changeValue is immutable by rule
1NoneOverwriteCorrections; history unimportant
2FullNew row per versionAudit and historical reporting
3One previous valueExtra columnOnly current and previous matter
4Full, separateHistory tableCurrent and history have different access needs
5Profile history plus currentMini-dimensionFast-changing profiles
6Full plus current1 + 2 + 3Need both views in one table
7Full plus currentDual keysNeed both views without restating history

Bitemporal modeling

Two timelines exist: valid time (when a fact was true in the real world) and transaction time (when the warehouse learned it). Regulators often need both, for example “what did we believe on 30 June about Ravi's city on 1 June?”

Production problems to plan for

  • Late-arriving and out-of-order changes
  • Duplicate effective timestamps and several changes in one day
  • Retroactive corrections that must restate history
  • Surrogate-key lookup failures
  • Overlapping intervals and two “current” rows
  • Merged or deleted customers

Types 0 to 4 are widely standardized. Types 5 to 7 vary slightly between authors, so document exactly how your implementation works.

Bill Inmon's approach is top-down: first build a central, normalized (usually 3NF) enterprise data warehouse that integrates every source into one subject-oriented, non-volatile, time-variant store. Departmental data marts are then fed from it.

Source systems→Staging→Normalized EDW (3NF)→Data marts (dimensional)→BI and reports

Sample EDW tables (banking)

PARTY(party_id, party_type, name, date_of_birth)
ACCOUNT(account_id, product_id, branch_id, open_date, status)
PARTY_ACCOUNT_ROLE(party_id, account_id, role, valid_from, valid_to)   -- resolves M:N
CARD(card_id, account_id, card_type, status)
TXN(txn_id, account_id, txn_ts, amount, currency_code)
BRANCH(branch_id, branch_name, city_code)
StrengthsLimits
One consistent enterprise view; strong integration and data qualitySlow to deliver first value; heavy up-front modeling
Marts are rebuilt from one trusted sourceBusiness users cannot query 3NF easily; marts are required
Fits regulated enterprises that need a single version of truthSource changes can ripple through the integrated model

M:N in Inmon: resolved with associative tables such as PARTY_ACCOUNT_ROLE, with effective dates.

Data Vault separates three things that change at different speeds: who the business entities are (Hub), how they relate (Link) and what we know about them over time (Satellite). Example, a school: the register of student names (hubs), the class enrolments (links), and a diary of each student's changing details (satellites).

Sample rows

Hub (business key only)

customer_hkcustomer_idload_dtsrecord_source
a1f3…C1012026-11-01CORE
b92c…C1022026-11-01CORE

Satellite (every change adds a row; hashdiff detects change)

customer_hkload_dtsnamecityhashdiff
a1f3…2026-11-01RaviHyderabad91d0…
a1f3…2026-11-16RaviMumbai7ce4…

Building blocks

ElementPurpose
Hash keyDeterministic key from the business key, so loads run in parallel without lookups
HashdiffHash of descriptive columns; a new satellite row is inserted only when it changes
Load date and record sourceAudit: when and from which system each row arrived
Effectivity satelliteTracks when a relationship (link) starts and ends
Multi-active satelliteSeveral current rows per key, such as multiple phone numbers
PIT tablePre-joins satellites for a snapshot date to speed point-in-time queries
Bridge tablePre-joins links to simplify traversal across many relationships
Raw VaultSource data loaded unchanged, insert-only
Business VaultBusiness rules and derived data applied on top of the Raw Vault
Information martsStar schemas or views built from the vault for reporting
StrengthsLimits
Full audit trail and history; source changes usually add new satellitesMore tables and joins; not designed for direct dashboard queries
Parallel, repeatable, insert-only loadsNeeds marts, PIT and bridge tables for performance
Integrates many sources without changing existing structuresHigher skill and tooling requirement

M:N in Data Vault: every relationship is a link, so many-to-many is represented naturally; the vault does not remove M:N, it records every association with dates.

These are not rivals. They solve different problems: Kimball serves analysis, Inmon serves enterprise integration, and Data Vault serves auditable, change-tolerant ingestion.

If your situation is…Choose

Sources→Raw / Data Vault→Business rules→Kimball marts→Semantic layer (Denodo, BI)→Reports, AI
ApproachIdeaGood forCaution

Part 5 · Meaning, metadata and governance

Three banking applications call the same person CUST_ID, CARD_HOLDER_ID and PARTY_REF.

ConceptQuestion it answersExample
Canonical modelHow do systems exchange information consistently?One format where all three IDs map to partyId
Semantic modelWhat does this data mean to the business?Active Customer = holds at least one qualifying active product at the report date
OntologyWhat concepts exist, how are they related, what can be inferred?LoanAccount is a kind of FinancialAccount; Person holds FinancialAccount
MDMWhich records are the same real-world entity?C101, H202 and P1001 are one person
Data dictionaryWhat does each field mean?Customer_Status values and who owns them

Canonical model

{ "partyId": "P1001", "partyType": "PERSON",
  "identifiers": [ {"system":"CORE","id":"C101"}, {"system":"CARDS","id":"H202"} ] }

With N systems, point-to-point mapping needs up to N×N transformations; a canonical model needs N. It does not decide identity (that is MDM) and should be versioned with an anti-corruption layer so each system's quirks stay out of the shared contract.

Semantic model

Defines business names, joins, hierarchies, metrics and access rules once. Delivered through BI models (Qlik master items), a metrics layer or data virtualization. A good definition states qualifying products, status rules, date logic, exclusions and aggregation behavior.

Denodo (data virtualization)

View layerRole
Base viewsMirror source tables
Integration viewsCombine and standardize sources
Business (derived) viewsGoverned, business-named views for consumers
Policies and cachingSecurity, performance, query delegation to the source

Ontology ladder

Glossary→Taxonomy→Thesaurus (SKOS)→Ontology (OWL)→Knowledge graph

A glossary lists terms; a taxonomy adds parent-child; a thesaurus adds synonyms; an ontology adds classes, properties and rules; a knowledge graph fills the ontology with real data. Facts are stored as triples (subject – predicate – object), for example Ravi – holds – Account A101, queried with SPARQL. FIBO is the well-known finance ontology.

Denodo is a data virtualization layer. It does not usually copy data; it exposes sources through views that users query as one database. The semantic modeling is the work of defining those views and their business meaning.

Steps

#StepWhat you doExample
1ConnectCreate data sources and import tables as base viewsSnowflake loans, Oracle core banking
2CleanRename, cast and filter; hide technical columnsCUST_ID → customer_id
3IntegrateJoin and union base views in integration views; map to canonical keysCustomer from core and cards
4Define business meaningBusiness views with agreed names, derived measures and hierarchiesActive Customer, Net Exposure
5Relationships and associationsDeclare links between views for self-service toolsCustomer to Account
6SecureApply role-based restrictions on columns and rows, plus maskingBranch staff see their region only
7PerformanceRely on delegation to sources; add cache or summary views for heavy joinsDaily balance summary
8Publish and documentExpose by JDBC, ODBC, REST or OData; record in the data catalog with ownersQlik and Power BI connect to business views
9Version and promoteUse revision control, then promote dev → test → prodRelease of Customer 360 view

Layers

Base views (mirror)→Integration views (combine)→Business views (meaning)→Consumers

Denodo is not the system of record and not a replacement for a warehouse where data must be historised or audited.

Data profiling: verify assumptions with data

CheckQuestion for CORE_CUSTOMER
Row countHow many records exist?
NullsIs Customer_ID ever missing?
UniquenessAre IDs duplicated?
DomainWhich status values exist?
PatternDo IDs follow the expected format?
DistributionIs any city unusually frequent?
Referential integrityDo account customer IDs resolve?
Temporal validityAre there future or contradictory dates?
Cross-system consistencyDoes the same customer have conflicting attributes?
FreshnessWhen was the latest update?
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows,
       COUNT_IF(customer_id IS NULL) AS null_ids,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)   AS unique_ids,
       MIN(update_ts) AS earliest_update, MAX(update_ts) AS latest_update
FROM raw.core_customer;

A model does not say how data arrives. The STTM does.

Part 6 · Building it on real platforms

A model on paper does nothing until it is created on a platform. The skill is to keep one logical model and translate it into each platform's physical features. It is like an architect's blueprint (logical) and the builder's choices of bricks and wiring for each site (physical).

The one-page workflow

Conceptual (business words)→Logical in ERwin / ER/Studio→Physical per platform→Forward engineer DDL→Deploy with CI/CD→Reverse engineer to verify→Publish to catalog and semantic layer

One bank, three levels of the same model

Conceptual: only business things and verbs, no columns.

Logical (Data Vault 2.0 style): keys, links and history, but no platform types yet.

Physical (Snowflake): platform types, schemas and tuning.

CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS DV_RAW;
CREATE TABLE DV_RAW.HUB_CUSTOMER (
  HK_CUSTOMER  BINARY(32)    NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  CUSTOMER_ID  VARCHAR(34)   NOT NULL,
  LOAD_DTS     TIMESTAMP_NTZ NOT NULL,
  REC_SRC      VARCHAR(50)   NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE DV_RAW.LINK_CUSTOMER_ACCOUNT (
  HK_LINK_CUSTOMER_ACCOUNT BINARY(32) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  HK_CUSTOMER BINARY(32) NOT NULL REFERENCES DV_RAW.HUB_CUSTOMER(HK_CUSTOMER),
  HK_ACCOUNT  BINARY(32) NOT NULL,
  LOAD_DTS TIMESTAMP_NTZ NOT NULL, REC_SRC VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE DV_RAW.SAT_ACCOUNT_BALANCES (
  HK_ACCOUNT BINARY(32) NOT NULL, LOAD_DTS TIMESTAMP_NTZ NOT NULL,
  HASHDIFF BINARY(32), BALANCE_AMOUNT NUMBER(18,4), CURRENCY_CD VARCHAR(3),
  REC_SRC VARCHAR(50), PRIMARY KEY (HK_ACCOUNT, LOAD_DTS))
  CLUSTER BY (HK_ACCOUNT, LOAD_DTS);

Integration pattern in a bank

Core banking→CDC (Qlik Replicate)→Raw / Bronze→Vault / Silver→Marts / Gold→Denodo semantic views→Qlik, Power BI, APIs

Rule of thumb: model once, adapt the physical layer per platform, and keep the catalog, masking and lineage identical in meaning everywhere.

Compare it with building plans. Forward engineering builds the house from the plan. Reverse engineering draws the plan from an existing house.

Forward engineeringReverse engineering
DirectionModel → DDL → databaseDatabase or DDL → model
Use whenNew build or approved changeLegacy system with no documentation, or checking drift
ToolsERwin Forward Engineer, ER/Studio generate DDL, SQL scripts under version controlERwin Reverse Engineer, ER/Studio import from database, catalog or DDL files
OutputCREATE and ALTER scripts, indexes, commentsEntities, columns, keys and inferred relationships
Watch outPlatform-specific types and options; do not hand-edit generated DDLInferred relationships need confirmation; business names and definitions are missing

Complete and compare

Compare and merge (ERwin Complete Compare, ER/Studio Compare and Merge) shows the differences between the model and the live database, so you choose which side wins. This is how drift is caught.

Round-trip process

Change request→Update logical model→Update physical model→Compare to dev→Generate ALTER→Review and test→Deploy→Reverse engineer and compare to confirm

Do not reverse engineer and then call the result a logical model. It is a physical picture; add business names, definitions and cardinality by hand.

TopicWhat it coversTypical tooling
Governance operating modelOwners, stewards, custodians, policies, issue management; aligned to DAMA-DMBOKCouncil, RACI, policies
Business glossaryAgreed business terms and definitionsCollibra
Data catalogue and lineageWhat data exists, where it came from, who uses itCollibra, lineage tools
ClassificationPublic, internal, confidential, PII, PHICatalogue tags, masking policies

MDMGolden record via matching and survivorshipMDM platform
Reference dataGoverned code sets (currency, country, status)Reference-data hub

Master data management in four steps

Match (exact and fuzzy)→Merge into golden record→Apply survivorship rules→Publish with crosswalks

Survivorship decides which value wins when sources disagree (most recent, most trusted source, most complete). Crosswalks map each system's ID to the master ID. Hierarchies such as household or legal entity are mastered too.

Three kinds of metadata

KindExample
BusinessDefinition, owner, glossary term
TechnicalData type, table, column, key
OperationalLoad time, row count, job status

Metadata is data about data: the label on the box. Without it nobody knows what is inside, who owns it, or whether it can be trusted.

TypeExamplesWho maintains it
BusinessDefinition, owner, steward, glossary term, sensitivityBusiness and stewards
TechnicalTable, column, type, key, partition, lineageData engineers and modelers
OperationalLoad time, row counts, job status, quality scorePipelines and platform
SocialRatings, usage, commentsUsers

Lifecycle

Capture (scan sources)→Harvest into catalog→Enrich (definitions, owners, tags)→Link (glossary to columns)→Lineage→Publish and search→Review and recertify

In practice

  • Model as the source: definitions and keys entered in ERwin or ER/Studio are exported or harvested into the catalog (Collibra, Purview, Alation, Dataplex, Unity Catalog, Glue Data Catalog).
  • Automatic harvest: catalogs scan schemas on a schedule; lineage comes from pipeline and query logs.
  • Tags drive policy: a column tagged PII triggers masking automatically.
  • Ownership: every dataset has an owner and steward; unowned data is reported.
  • Change control: a schema change updates metadata through the same release as the code.

Memory hook: label, link, lineage, learn. Label every asset, link it to the glossary, trace its lineage, and learn from usage.

Metadata quality is itself measured: percentage of columns with definitions, of datasets with owners, and of PII columns tagged.

Governance answers four questions: Who owns it? Who can see it? How good is it? Can we prove it?

Data stewardDefines terms, resolves quality issues

Part 7 · Change, quality and trust

Change data capture (CDC) reads the source database log and emits each insert, update and delete as an event.

ConcernQuestionPractice
OrderingWhat if events arrive out of order?Apply by sequence number or log position, not arrival time
DeletesHow is a removal represented?Soft-delete flag or tombstone event
IdempotencyWhat if an event is applied twice?MERGE on key; reruns must not create duplicates
DeliveryAt-least-once or exactly-once?Assume at-least-once and make loads idempotent
Late dataWhat if yesterday's event arrives today?Reprocess the affected window; restate history

Part 9 · Practice and reference

Six questions to ask before any design

  1. What is the business process?
  2. What is the grain?
  3. Which entities and relationships, with cardinality and optionality?
  4. Which keys and history requirements?
  5. What is the target workload: OLTP, EDW, reporting, audit or streaming?
  6. How will correctness be verified?

Tricky questions

QuestionAnswer
Can a fact table have no measures?Yes. A factless fact records that an event happened or a condition existed; you count rows.
Can a dimension have several rows for one business key?Yes, with SCD Type 2 each version is a row with its own surrogate key.
Can a fact table hold a text identifier?Yes, as a degenerate dimension such as a transaction number.
Is every numeric column a fact?No. Quantities that describe an entity (age, rating) are usually attributes; facts are measures of events.
Does Data Vault eliminate many-to-many?No. Links represent M:N and record every association.
Does 3NF always mean better performance?No. It protects writes; analytical reads often need joins or denormalized marts.
Is a primary key always a surrogate key?No. It can be natural or composite.
Can a fact join directly to another fact?Avoid it; aggregate each to a common grain and drill across conformed dimensions.
Can a dimension serve several facts?Yes, that is what makes it conformed.
What do you ask first before designing a fact table?What is the grain?

23 blocks covering the associative engine, load scripts, data modeling in Qlik, set analysis, security and production support. Tap a block to open it.

Part 1 · Foundations and architecture

Imagine a bank with 100 branches. Management wants one dashboard that answers: today's transaction volume, branches with the highest deposits, new customers, loan disbursement trend, branches below target and this month versus last year. Qlik Sense is the tool that loads the data, models it and lets users click through it freely. This page follows that bank from source systems to production dashboards.

Sources in our story: Oracle (accounts), SQL Server (transactions), Snowflake (analytical data), Excel (monthly targets).

AreaQlikViewQlik Sense (Windows)Qlik Cloud Analytics

VisualsTraditional dashboardsResponsive, modern chartsModern cloud analytics
ScriptingLoad scriptLoad scriptLoad script
EngineAssociativeAssociativeAssociative
InfrastructureCustomer-managedCustomer-managed on WindowsQlik-managed SaaS
AdministrationQMCQMCCloud administration and spaces

Learning roadmap

Foundations→Architecture→Loading→Scripting→QVD→Modeling→Set analysis→Front end→Security→Performance→Production

Picture a bank officer's desk with every file linked by string. Pick one file (Hyderabad) and the strings pull every connected file forward, while unrelated files fall back.

CustomerCityProduct
RaviHyderabadLoan
PriyaMumbaiCard
AnilHyderabadSavings
MeeraDelhiLoan

Select Hyderabad: Ravi and Anil stay possible; Priya and Meera become excluded. Products also update: Loan and Savings stay possible, Card is excluded.

ColorMeaning
GreenSelected
WhitePossible (associated with the selection)
GreyExcluded

Select, associate, recalculate

User selects→Engine associates values→Possible and excluded values update→Every chart recalculates

Key difference: traditional BI often sends a new query to the source for each click. In a normal imported Qlik app, selections work on data already loaded in the engine. The distinction is the associative selection model, not merely that data is in memory.

RolePurpose
Central nodeCoordinates administration and repository
Rim nodeExtra capacity for workloads
Consumer nodeServes interactive dashboards to users
Reload nodeRuns scheduled reloads
Failover candidateCan take over central duties under supported setups

Example: 500 users and 50 apps could run as one central node, two consumer nodes and one reload node. Why separate reloads? A heavy reload competes for CPU and memory with users clicking dashboards.

Memory hook, PERS: Proxy = Entry, Engine = Calculate, Repository = Metadata, Scheduler = Reload. Printing is the extra P.

Service placement, network paths and persistence vary by deployment, so treat the diagram as conceptual.

SpaceUse
PersonalIndividual development and exploration
SharedCollaboration and app development
ManagedGoverned consumption and controlled publication
DataData integration and data-product workflows, where available
TopicWindowsCloud
Admin consoleQMCCloud management console and spaces
ScalingYou size and add nodesManaged by Qlik
ServicesQPS, QES, QRS, QSS, QPRNot administered as node services
Private dataDirect network accessData gateway for private or on-premises sources
SecuritySection Access, security rules, streamsSection Access, roles, space permissions

In-memory versus Direct Query: traditional apps load data into the engine on reload. Supported Direct Query approaches query an external database instead; features and limits depend on platform and release.

Part 2 · Loading data

The load script is a list of instructions that brings data into Qlik, shapes it and builds the data model.

1. LOAD from a file

Customers:
LOAD CustomerID, CustomerName, City
FROM [lib://BankFiles/Customers.csv]
(txt, utf8, embedded labels, delimiter is ',');

2. SQL SELECT from a database

LIB CONNECT TO 'BANK_ORACLE';
Accounts:
SQL SELECT ACCOUNT_ID, CUSTOMER_ID, BALANCE
FROM BANK.ACCOUNTS;

The query runs in the source database and only the result is loaded.

3. Inline load: small reference data

Region:
LOAD * INLINE [
RegionID, RegionName
1, North
2, South
];

4. Resident load: from a table already in memory

AccountSummary:
LOAD AccountID, Sum(Amount) AS TotalAmount
RESIDENT Transactions
GROUP BY AccountID;
DROP TABLE Transactions;

Use it for aggregation, sorting with ORDER BY, multi-stage steps and reuse of intermediate tables.

5. Preceding load: transform on the way in

Transactions:
LOAD TransactionID, AccountID, Amount,
     If(Amount >= 1000, 'High', 'Normal') AS AmountBand;
LOAD TransactionID, AccountID, Num#(AmountText) AS Amount
FROM [lib://BankFiles/Transactions.csv]
(txt, utf8, embedded labels, delimiter is ',');

The lower LOAD runs first; the upper LOAD transforms its output.

PrecedingResident
Chains transformationsReads an existing logical table
Often avoids an intermediate tableIntermediate table is available for reuse
No ORDER BYSupports ORDER BY
Sequential field derivationGrouping, sorting, staging

Hook: Preceding = transform on the way in. Resident = transform after it is in memory.

StatementPurpose
LOAD / SQL SELECTBring data in
INLINEData typed in the script
RESIDENTLoad from an existing Qlik table
MAPPING LOADCreate a lookup for ApplyMap
BINARYLoad another app's data model (must come first)
BUFFERCache supported load results
CONCATENATE / NOCONCATENATEAppend rows / prevent automatic append
JOIN / KEEPMerge tables / filter tables
CROSSTABLEUnpivot columns into rows
GENERICSplit attribute-value data into tables
INTERVALMATCHMatch values to ranges
FIRSTLimit rows loaded
DISTINCT / WHERE / GROUP BY / ORDER BYDeduplicate, filter, aggregate, sort

CrossTable: columns to rows

Source has Branch, Jan, Feb. We want one row per branch and month.

CrossTable(Month, Sales, 1)
LOAD Branch, Jan, Feb
INLINE [
Branch, Jan, Feb
B01, 100, 150
B02, 200, 250
];
BranchMonthSales
B01Jan100
B01Feb150
B02Jan200
B02Feb250

Binary load

BINARY [lib://BankApps/BaseBanking.qvf];

It must be the first data-loading statement (some SET statements may precede it) and depends on platform support.

IntervalMatch

Assign each transaction to the interest-rate period valid on its date.

Generic load

Turns rows like (C101, City, Hyderabad) and (C101, Segment, Gold) into separate attribute tables, which often need consolidating afterwards.

A QVD is Qlik's native, compressed data file, very fast to read. It works like a prepared ingredient kept in the fridge, so each dish (app) does not start from raw vegetables (the source).

// Store
Customers:
LOAD CustomerID, CustomerName, City
FROM [lib://BankFiles/Customers.csv] (txt, utf8, embedded labels, delimiter is ',');
STORE Customers INTO [lib://QVDStorage/Customers.qvd] (qvd);
DROP TABLE Customers;

// Read (optimized)
Customers:
LOAD CustomerID, CustomerName, City
FROM [lib://QVDStorage/Customers.qvd] (qvd);

// Standard (not optimized): a transformation is applied
Customers:
LOAD CustomerID, Upper(CustomerName) AS CustomerName, City
FROM [lib://QVDStorage/Customers.qvd] (qvd);

Optimized load

An optimized read bypasses row-by-row processing. Calculated fields, some WHERE conditions, DISTINCT and some transformations break it. Simple renaming and some filters, including a supported WHERE Exists() form, can stay optimized.

FunctionReturns
QvdCreateTime()When the QVD was created
QvdNoOfRecords()Row count
QvdNoOfFields()Field count
QvdFieldName()Field name by position
QvdTableName()Stored table name

Why not query Snowflake every time? QVDs reduce source load, speed reloads, give reusable layers and make incremental loads possible. QVD is data; QVF is the application file.

A full reload re-reads everything. If a table has 100 million rows and 50,000 change daily, reloading all of it hourly wastes time and money.

PatternExampleApproach
Insert onlyNew transactionsAppend unseen records
Insert and updateCustomer detailsMerge changed rows
Insert, update, deleteAccount masterHandle all three
CDC basedOracle or SQL Server change captureApply captured changes
Partition basedDaily transaction partitionsReload affected periods

Insert and update pattern

LET vWatermark = '2026-11-15 00:00:00';
LIB CONNECT TO 'BANK_SQLSERVER';

ChangedCustomers:
SQL SELECT CustomerID, CustomerName, City, ModifiedTimestamp
FROM dbo.Customers
WHERE ModifiedTimestamp >= '$(vWatermark)';

Concatenate (ChangedCustomers)
LOAD CustomerID, CustomerName, City, ModifiedTimestamp
FROM [lib://QVDStorage/Customers.qvd] (qvd)
WHERE NOT Exists(CustomerID);

STORE ChangedCustomers INTO [lib://QVDStorage/Customers.qvd] (qvd);

Changed rows load first; Exists(CustomerID) then stops the old QVD versions of those customers from loading.

Production checklist

  • One latest row per key; deduplicate changes.
  • Reliable watermark with overlap, or a CDC position.
  • Handle deletes explicitly.
  • Write the new QVD safely before replacing the old one.
  • Move the watermark only after a successful commit.
  • Make retries idempotent.

Taking the last row with Peek() as the watermark is only safe if the data is explicitly ordered and the IDs suit it. Store the last committed watermark separately.

Partial reload uses Add, Replace and Merge prefixes to refresh selected tables without a full reload. CDC tools such as Qlik Replicate feed changes continuously, and the QVD layer applies them.

Part 3 · Combining data and modeling

Customers: C1 Ravi, C2 Priya, C3 Anil. Orders: O1 (C1, 500), O2 (C1, 700), O3 (C2, 300), O4 (C4, 900).

Join typeKeepsResult here
InnerMatching rows onlyC1 twice, C2 once
LeftAll customers, matching ordersAdds C3 with no order
RightAll orders, matching customersAdds O4 with no customer
OuterEverything from bothAll of the above
INNER JOIN (Customers)
LOAD * INLINE [
OrderID, CustomerID, Amount
O1, C1, 500
O2, C1, 700
O3, C2, 300
O4, C4, 900
];
JOINKEEP
OutputOne merged tableTwo separate tables
Row multiplicationPossibleNot from the join
Common fieldsAct as join keysUsed to filter
Typical useEnrich a tableReduce data, keep associations

Inner Keep: Customers keeps C1 and C2; Orders keeps O1, O2, O3; the tables stay separate and associate on CustomerID. Left Keep keeps the left table and filters the right; Right Keep does the reverse.

Qlik joins on all fields with the same name, not an explicit ON clause. Two shared field names silently create a composite join.

Hook: JOIN = merge columns. CONCATENATE = add rows. KEEP = filter without merging.

Qlik automatically concatenates tables that have identical field names, even if the table labels differ.

Sales:
LOAD * INLINE [
Year, Amount
2025, 100
];
CONCATENATE (Sales)
LOAD * INLINE [
Year, Amount
2026, 200
];

NoConcatenate
CustomersCopy:
LOAD * RESIDENT Customers;

ApplyMap looks up one value, like asking "which city is B01?" without joining tables.

BranchMap:
MAPPING LOAD * INLINE [
BranchID, BranchName
B01, Hyderabad
B02, Mumbai
];
Transactions:
LOAD TransactionID, BranchID,
     ApplyMap('BranchMap', BranchID, 'Unknown') AS BranchName,
     Amount
INLINE [
TransactionID, BranchID, Amount
T1, B01, 500
T2, B02, 700
T3, B03, 300
];
ApplyMapJoin
Returns one mapped valueCan bring many columns
Never multiplies rowsCan multiply rows
Needs a mapping tableNeeds a source table
Best for simple lookupsBest for complex enrichment

Here B03 returns Unknown, the default, and no rows are lost or duplicated.

Qlik associates tables automatically through fields with exactly the same name. No SQL join is written.

CUSTOMER (CustomerID)→ACCOUNT (AccountID, CustomerID)→TRANSACTION (TransactionID, AccountID)

Best practice is a star schema: one fact table with dimensions around it, as described in the Data modeling page (grain first, then facts and dimensions).

ProblemMeaningFix
Synthetic keyTwo tables share two or more fields; Qlik builds a $Syn keyRename fields that should not associate, build a composite key, use a link table or fix the grain
Circular referenceSeveral association paths between tables, for example Customer → Account → Branch → CustomerUnderstand the business paths; break or rename the wrong association
Many-to-manyBoth tables repeat the keyBridge or link table at the right grain
AutoNumberHash128(CustomerID, BranchID) AS %CustomerBranchKey

Link tables

When several facts share several dimensions, a link table holds the distinct key combinations and each fact carries one link key. It resolves synthetic keys, but adds complexity and memory use.

Canonical calendar

A loan has application, approval and disbursement dates. A canonical calendar lets one date selection work across all three through a date bridge with a DateType field. Careful: one loan appears several times in the bridge, so aggregate with care.

Do not remove a circular-reference warning by renaming fields at random. Fix the business relationship first.

FunctionUse
Today(), Now()Current date, current timestamp
Date(), Timestamp()Format a numeric value
Date#(), Timestamp#()Interpret text as a date or timestamp
MonthStart(), MonthEnd(), YearStart(), WeekStart()Period boundaries
AddMonths(), AddYears()Shift dates
NetWorkDays()Working days
Floor()Remove the time fraction
Date(Today(), 'DD/MM/YYYY')            // formats a number
Date#('16/11/2026', 'DD/MM/YYYY')      // interprets text

Hook: a # sign means interpret the input. No # means format the output.

Master calendar

Calendar:
LOAD Date(DateID) AS TxnDate,
     Year(DateID) AS Year, Month(DateID) AS Month,
     MonthName(DateID) AS MonthYear, Week(DateID) AS Week,
     QuarterName(DateID) AS Quarter;
LOAD Date($(vMinDate) + IterNo() - 1) AS DateID
AUTOGENERATE 1
WHILE $(vMinDate) + IterNo() - 1 <= $(vMaxDate);

vMinDate and vMaxDate must be numeric Qlik dates. Convert timestamps to date-only keys so the calendar associates correctly.

Part 4 · Expressions

Syntax: Sum({$<Year={2026}>} Sales). Read it as: sum Sales for the current selection, but force Year to 2026.

PartMeaning
Sum()The aggregation
{ }The set expression
$Current selections
< >Modifier
Year={2026}Field and the value it is forced to
IdentifierMeaning
$Current selections
1All records, ignoring selections
1-$Everything except the current selection
$1 / $2Previous selection states
$_1Forward selection state
StateAAn alternate state
ExpressionResult
Sum({1} Sales)Total, ignoring all selections
Sum({$<Year={2026}>} Sales)Only 2026
Sum({$<Year={2025,2026}>} Sales)2025 and 2026
Sum({$<Region=>} Sales)Ignore the Region selection, keep others
Sum({$<Region-={'South'}>} Sales)Remove South from the current Region set
Sum({$<Year={2026}, Product={'Loan'}>} Amount)Two conditions
Sum({$<Year={"$(=Max({1} Year))"}>} Amount)Latest year
Count({$<CustomerID=P({$<Product={'Loan'}>} CustomerID)>} DISTINCT CustomerID)Customers who hold a loan

Date examples

// Current month (numeric dates)
Sum({<TxnDate={">=$(=Num(MonthStart(Today())))<=$(=Num(MonthEnd(Today())))"}>} Amount)
// Previous month
Sum({<TxnDate={">=$(=Num(MonthStart(AddMonths(Today(),-1))))<$(=Num(MonthStart(Today())))"}>} Amount)
// Year to date
Sum({<TxnDate={">=$(=Num(YearStart(Today())))<=$(=Num(Today()))"}>} Amount)

These assume TxnDate holds whole dates. For timestamps use an exclusive upper bound at the start of the next period.

OperatorMeaningHook
+Unioncombine
*Intersectioncommon
-Differencesubtract
/Symmetric differenceeither side only

P() returns possible values, E() returns excluded values, within the set you give.

Sum(If(Year=2026, Sales)) tests each row. Sum({<Year={2026}>} Sales) defines the set first. They are not interchangeable; set analysis is usually clearer for KPIs, and If() still suits row-level conditions.

Question: what is the highest total any single branch produced?

Max(Aggr(Sum(Amount), Branch))
BranchTotal
Hyderabad50,000
Mumbai80,000
Delhi60,000

Aggr first totals each branch, then Max picks ₹80,000.

ExpressionMeaning
Sum(TOTAL Amount)Ignore chart dimensions, respect selections
Sum(Amount) / Sum(TOTAL Amount)Each row's share of the total
Sum(TOTAL <Region> Amount)Ignore other dimensions, keep Region
FunctionPurpose
Above / Below / Before / AfterNeighboring rows or columns in a chart
RangeSum / RangeAvgSum or average a range
RowNo / RankPosition and ranking
FirstSortedValueValue by sort weight
OnlyValue when exactly one distinct value exists
GetSelectedCount / GetFieldSelections / GetPossibleCountSelection information
Match / WildMatch / Pick / ClassMatching and bucketing
RangeSum(Above(Sum(Amount), 0, RowNo()))   // running total

A running total depends on sort order and column segments; test it with several dimensions before release.

SET vCurrency = INR;
SET vExample = 5+5;     // stores the text 5+5
LET vExample = 5+5;     // evaluates and stores 10
LET vToday = Today(1);
// use:  $(vExample)

Reusable KPI: store Sum(Amount) in a variable and write $(vTotalAmount) in charts. Watch quoting, nested expansion and whether the variable holds expression text or a result.

Hook: SET stores text. LET evaluates.

Part 5 · Front end, security and reporting

ItemUse
KPI objectsRevenue, transactions, target attainment
Bar and line chartsComparison, trend, ranking
Tables (pivot and straight)Detailed operational reporting
MapsBranch and regional performance
Master itemsReusable dimensions, measures and visualizations
Drill-downHierarchy: Country → State → City → Branch
Cyclic dimensionSwitch between Branch, Product, Channel
BookmarksSave a selection state
Alternate statesCompare two selection contexts side by side

Master measure example: define Count(DISTINCT TransactionID) once as Total Transactions and reuse it on every sheet, so a change is made in one place.

Dashboard design for a bank

  • Top row: KPI tiles (volume, deposits, new customers, target attainment).
  • Middle: trend lines and branch ranking.
  • Bottom: detail table and map with drill-down.
  • Use consistent colors, readable labels and few filters.

Also learn containers, buttons, reference lines, conditional show and hide, dynamic titles, color expressions, tooltips, storytelling, extensions, themes, mashups and accessibility.

SECTION ACCESS;
LOAD * INLINE [
ACCESS, USERID, REGION
ADMIN, INTERNAL\SA_SCHEDULER, *
USER, DOMAIN\RAVI, NORTH
USER, DOMAIN\PRIYA, SOUTH
];
SECTION APPLICATION;
Sales:
LOAD * INLINE [
REGION, Amount
NORTH, 1000
SOUTH, 2000
EAST, 3000
];

Ravi sees only North, Priya only South. This is an illustration of Windows-style identities; syntax, wildcards and service accounts must be validated for your deployment. In Qlik Cloud, supported user identifiers or groups are used instead of Windows domain identities.

LayerControls
Platform permissions (security rules, spaces, streams)Which apps and actions a user can reach
Section AccessWhich data rows or fields the user can see

Precautions

  • Check field-name and value case.
  • Test with dedicated non-production users.
  • Keep administrator and reload identities in the table so reloads still work.
  • Do not lock yourself out of the app.

Hook: Section Access = which rows. Platform permissions = which apps.

NPrinting turns Qlik apps into distributed reports, like a bank sending each branch manager their own monthly pack.

Connection to app→Filter→Report template→Recipients and groups→Publish task and trigger→Delivery
PieceRole
ConnectionLinks NPrinting to a Qlik app
FilterLimits data, e.g. one branch per recipient
TemplateExcel, PDF or PowerPoint layout
Recipient or groupWho receives it
Publish taskGenerates and sends (email, folder, hub)
TriggerSchedule or event, e.g. after reload
On-demandUser requests a report from the app

Typical issues: task failure (check connection, filter and permissions), empty report (filter returns nothing), wrong recipients (group membership), template field mismatch after an app change.

Part 6 · Performance and production

ProblemImprovement
Slow source extractionPush suitable filters to the source SQL
Repeated source readsReusable QVD layers
Heavy transformationsPrecalculate where suitable
Duplicate rowsFix grain and deduplicate
Long string keysCompact numeric keys
Unused columnsLoad only what you need
Complex joinsApplyMap, Keep or associations
High-cardinality timestampsSplit into date and time
Reloading everythingIncremental loads
Lost optimized QVD readsKeep reads simple, transform later

Qlik stores data in a compressed, column-oriented, in-memory form. Memory depends on rows, distinct values, fields, relationships, concurrent users, calculation complexity and reload activity.

AutoNumberHash128(CustomerID, AccountID) AS %CustomerAccountKey

AutoNumber values are not stable across separate reloads or apps. For persistent cross-app keys, use deterministic hashing of normalized inputs.

Dashboards

Avoid nested Aggr(), huge straight tables and high-cardinality dimensions. Pre-aggregate when the grain allows (for example a daily branch summary), but keep detail where users need transaction drill-down.

Scheduler or automation trigger→Connect and extract→Run script, build model→Successful reload→Dashboard available
IssueWhere to look
Reload failedReload log, source connection, SQL, credentials
App opens slowlyApp size, concurrency, engine resources
No dataReload status, filters, associations, Section Access
Wrong KPIGrain, join multiplication, set expressions
DuplicatesSynthetic keys, many-to-many joins, wrong concatenation
Out of memoryData volume, cardinality, concurrent load
Reload timeoutSource query, network, gateway, limits
QVD not foundPath, permissions, environment differences
Two apps disagreeFreshness, business logic, time zone, filters

Case: dashboard shows ₹2 crore, Snowflake shows ₹1 crore

  1. Compare record counts.
  2. Validate the grain of each table.
  3. Check joins for row multiplication.
  4. Check link or bridge tables for duplication.
  5. Verify date and time-zone filters.
  6. Inspect set analysis.
  7. Compare reload timestamps.
  8. Reconcile at TransactionID level.

A bigger Snowflake warehouse will not fix a Qlik modeling error. It can speed a query but not remove duplicated measures or wrong associations.

Part 7 · Practice and reference

QuestionShort answer
What happens when a user selects a value?The engine finds associated values, marks them possible, excludes the rest and recalculates every object.
QVD versus QVF?QVD is a data file; QVF is the application.
Why QVD instead of querying Snowflake each time?Fewer source hits, faster reloads, reusable layers, incremental loads.
Why do synthetic keys appear?Two tables share more than one field name.
Resolve a circular reference?Understand the business paths, then rename or break the extra association, or use a link table.
Join or Keep?Join to merge columns; Keep to filter while keeping tables separate.
Common cause of inflated measures?Join multiplication, many-to-many links or wrong grain.
Can set analysis ignore one field's selection?Yes: {$<Region=>}.
What if a reload fails?Check the log, connection, SQL and credentials; keep the last good data; retry idempotently.
Design for 500 million rows?QVD layers, incremental loads, star schema, numeric keys, pre-aggregation, separate reload node.
Master calendar versus canonical calendar?Master: one date role. Canonical: several date roles through a bridge with a type field.
Implement data security?Section Access for rows, plus space and security rules for apps.
Windows versus Cloud administration?Windows uses QMC and nodes; Cloud is managed with spaces and roles.
Optimize a slow chart?Reduce high-cardinality dimensions, avoid nested Aggr, precalculate, simplify the model.

Knowledge · Data platform

Snowflake

22 blocks on Snowflake, from architecture and warehouses to loading, streams, modeling, security, cost and the Qlik Replicate pipeline. Tap a block to open it.

Part 1 · Foundations

Snowflake is a managed cloud platform for analytics, data engineering and data sharing. The idea that sets it apart: data sits in one storage layer, and any number of independent compute clusters (called virtual warehouses) read it. Loading, transformation and reporting can each have their own compute and never fight over the same machine.

A bank makes the point. Say it has 10 million customers, 50 million accounts, 2 billion transactions, 500 branches, daily fraud analytics, regulatory reports and Qlik dashboards. If the nightly load and the 9 a.m. dashboards run on one server, they slow each other down. In Snowflake they run on different warehouses over the same data. One bank, one project (Customer 360, CASA, cards, loans, branch performance, fraud) is the thread through these notes.

Traditional databaseSnowflake
Storage and computeOften tied togetherSeparate; storage is managed for you
ScalingDepends on the setupResize a warehouse, or add clusters
Storage formatUsually row-oriented, built for transactionsColumnar, built for analysis
Workload isolationNeeds careful configurationOne warehouse per workload
JSONVariesNative (VARIANT)
AdministrationDBA-managed infrastructureManaged platform

Snowflake is built for analytics. I would not put the core banking ledger on it; that is an OLTP job.

Storage holds table data as compressed, columnar micro-partitions; you never manage the files. Compute is the virtual warehouses that run queries. Cloud services handle login, metadata, query optimization, security and transaction coordination. A way to remember it: store, compute, coordinate.

Objects, top down

Organization → account → databases → schemas → tables, views, stages, file formats, streams, tasks, procedures, functions. Warehouses belong to the account, not to a database.

CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS BANK_DWH;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS BANK_DWH.RAW;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS BANK_DWH.STAGING;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS BANK_DWH.CURATED;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS BANK_DWH.MART;

-- fully qualified name: DATABASE.SCHEMA.TABLE
SELECT * FROM BANK_DWH.CURATED.DIM_CUSTOMER;

SHOW SCHEMAS IN DATABASE BANK_DWH;
SELECT CURRENT_DATABASE(), CURRENT_SCHEMA(), CURRENT_ROLE(), CURRENT_WAREHOUSE();

A warehouse is a cluster of compute that you start, stop and resize. It only costs credits while it runs.

SizeCredits per hour (single cluster)
X-Small1
Small2
Medium4
Large8
X-Large16
2X-Large32
3X-Large64
4X-Large128

Each size up doubles the rate. These are credits, not money; the price per credit depends on your contract. Real use also depends on run time, cluster count and warehouse type.

CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS WH_BANK_ETL
  WITH WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'MEDIUM'
       AUTO_SUSPEND = 60
       AUTO_RESUME = TRUE
       INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE;

ALTER WAREHOUSE WH_BANK_ETL SET WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'LARGE';
ALTER WAREHOUSE WH_BANK_ETL SUSPEND;

Scale up or scale out?

If one query is slow, a bigger warehouse can help. If many queries are waiting in line, add clusters with a multi-cluster warehouse. People mix these up in interviews more than anything else.

CREATE WAREHOUSE WH_BANK_BI
  WITH WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'SMALL'
       MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1
       MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 3
       SCALING_POLICY = 'STANDARD'
       AUTO_SUSPEND = 60
       AUTO_RESUME = TRUE;

My usual setup is one warehouse per workload (ingest, transform, reporting), so a heavy load never slows a dashboard and the credits can be tracked by team.

Snowflake splits every table into micro-partitions, each holding roughly 50 to 500 MB of uncompressed data, and keeps metadata about each one: the minimum and maximum value of every column, and distinct counts. A query with a filter reads that metadata first and skips partitions that cannot match. That skipping is called pruning.

SELECT SUM(AMOUNT)
FROM BANK_DWH.CURATED.FACT_TRANSACTION
WHERE TRANSACTION_DATE >= '2026-11-01'
  AND TRANSACTION_DATE <  '2026-12-01';

The picture is simplified. In real tables partitions overlap, so pruning is rarely this clean. Data loaded in date order prunes well on date; data loaded in a random order does not.

Clustering

On very large tables, a clustering key keeps similar values together so pruning works better. It is maintained in the background and costs credits, so add it only after the query profile shows a lot of partitions scanned for a selective filter.

ALTER TABLE BANK_DWH.CURATED.FACT_TRANSACTION
  CLUSTER BY (TRANSACTION_DATE, BRANCH_ID);
SELECT SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION('BANK_DWH.CURATED.FACT_TRANSACTION','(TRANSACTION_DATE)');

Two related features. Search Optimization speeds up highly selective lookups (find one customer ID among billions of rows). Query Acceleration helps some scan-heavy queries by lending extra compute. Both cost credits, so measure first.

Part 2 · SQL and loading

GroupPurposeCommands
DDLDefine structuresCREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE
DMLChange dataINSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE
DQLRead dataSELECT
DCLControl accessGRANT, REVOKE
