CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER (
  CUSTOMER_ID   NUMBER(18,0),
  CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR(100),
  CITY          VARCHAR(50),
  CREATED_AT    TIMESTAMP_NTZ,
  UPDATED_AT    TIMESTAMP_NTZ);

INSERT INTO BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER (CUSTOMER_ID, CUSTOMER_NAME, CITY)
VALUES (101,'Ravi','Hyderabad'), (102,'Priya','Mumbai');
UPDATE BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER SET CITY = 'Bengaluru' WHERE CUSTOMER_ID = 101;
DELETE FROM BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_ID = 102;

MERGE

MERGE compares a source to a target and updates matching rows and inserts new ones in a single statement. It is the workhorse of loading.

MERGE INTO BANK_DWH.CURATED.CUSTOMER t
USING BANK_DWH.STAGING.CUSTOMER s
  ON t.CUSTOMER_ID = s.CUSTOMER_ID
WHEN MATCHED AND (t.CUSTOMER_NAME IS DISTINCT FROM s.CUSTOMER_NAME
               OR t.CITY          IS DISTINCT FROM s.CITY) THEN
  UPDATE SET t.CUSTOMER_NAME = s.CUSTOMER_NAME, t.CITY = s.CITY
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (CUSTOMER_ID, CUSTOMER_NAME, CITY)
  VALUES (s.CUSTOMER_ID, s.CUSTOMER_NAME, s.CITY);

That is a Type 1 overwrite. Two habits matter in production: remove duplicate keys from the source first (two source rows for one target row make the MERGE fail or behave unpredictably), and add a condition so unchanged rows are not rewritten.

Transactions

BEGIN;
UPDATE BANK_DWH.RAW.ACCOUNT SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 500 WHERE ACCOUNT_ID = 1001;
UPDATE BANK_DWH.RAW.ACCOUNT SET BALANCE = BALANCE + 500 WHERE ACCOUNT_ID = 1002;
COMMIT;

This shows the syntax only. A real funds transfer also needs balance checks, concurrency control, idempotency and ledger entries, and it belongs in an OLTP system.

TypeUse
NUMBER / DECIMALMoney and exact values
FLOATApproximate values only
VARCHARText
BOOLEANFlags
DATE, TIMECalendar date, time of day
TIMESTAMP_NTZNo time zone stored (a wall-clock value)
TIMESTAMP_LTZAn instant, shown in the session time zone
TIMESTAMP_TZValue plus its offset
VARIANT, OBJECT, ARRAYSemi-structured data
BINARYBytes, for example hash keys
GEOGRAPHY, GEOMETRYSpatial data
VECTOREmbeddings

Timestamp trap

A TIMESTAMP_NTZ does not say whether it holds UTC, India time or New York time. Agree on the source time zone and write the conversion down. Converting only works if the input really is what you say it is:

SELECT CONVERT_TIMEZONE('UTC', 'Asia/Kolkata', '2026-11-16 12:00:00'::TIMESTAMP_NTZ);
-- 2026-11-16 17:30:00

Keys

CREATE TABLE BANK_DWH.CURATED.DIM_BRANCH (
  BRANCH_SK   NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
  BRANCH_ID   VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE,
  BRANCH_NAME VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL);

On standard tables, primary key, unique and foreign key constraints are recorded but not enforced. NOT NULL is enforced. Hybrid tables behave differently and do enforce keys. So declaring a primary key does not stop duplicates; you enforce uniqueness in the load and test for it. The declaration is still worth making, because tools and optimizers read it.

Sequences and identity columns can leave gaps. Do not use them as business numbers that must be consecutive.

CREATE SEQUENCE BANK_DWH.CURATED.SEQ_CUSTOMER_SK START = 1 INCREMENT = 1;
SELECT BANK_DWH.CURATED.SEQ_CUSTOMER_SK.NEXTVAL;

Think of three parts. A stage is where the files wait. A file format says how to read them. COPY INTO loads them into a table.

Stage typeWhat it is
User stageBelongs to one user
Table stageBelongs to one table
Named internal stageReusable, Snowflake-managed storage
External stageA location in your cloud storage, such as S3
CREATE OR REPLACE FILE FORMAT BANK_DWH.RAW.CSV_FORMAT
  TYPE = CSV FIELD_DELIMITER = ',' SKIP_HEADER = 1
  FIELD_OPTIONALLY_ENCLOSED_BY = '"' NULL_IF = ('NULL','');

CREATE OR REPLACE STAGE BANK_DWH.RAW.BANK_STAGE
  FILE_FORMAT = BANK_DWH.RAW.CSV_FORMAT;

-- from SnowSQL or another client (PUT is a client command, not plain SQL)
PUT file:///tmp/customers.csv @BANK_DWH.RAW.BANK_STAGE AUTO_COMPRESS = TRUE;

COPY INTO BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER
FROM @BANK_DWH.RAW.BANK_STAGE
FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = BANK_DWH.RAW.CSV_FORMAT)
ON_ERROR = 'ABORT_STATEMENT';
OptionWhat it does
ON_ERRORWhat to do when a row or file fails
PATTERN, FILESChoose which files to load
PURGEDelete staged files after a successful load
FORCELoad files again even if already loaded
VALIDATION_MODECheck files without loading
MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAMEMatch file columns to table columns by name
COPY INTO BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER
FROM @BANK_DWH.RAW.BANK_STAGE
FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = BANK_DWH.RAW.CSV_FORMAT)
VALIDATION_MODE = RETURN_ERRORS;

The S3 version of this, with IAM and storage integrations, is on the AWS page.

Snowpipe loads files as they arrive in a stage, using serverless compute. The usual trigger on S3 is an event notification. Snowpipe Streaming skips files altogether: an application or connector (Kafka, a CDC tool) writes rows straight into a table through an API.

SnowpipeSnowpipe Streaming
InputStaged filesRows or events
File stagingNeededNot needed
ComputeServerlessManaged ingestion service
Best forFiles that keep arrivingLow-latency event data
Typical sourceS3 event notificationApplication, Kafka, CDC producer

If your source drops files, use Snowpipe. If it emits events, use streaming. If you load once a day, a scheduled COPY is simpler and cheaper to reason about. Channel types and limits for Streaming change between releases, so read the current documentation before designing around them.

A stream records the changes made to a table since the last time they were consumed. It does not read Oracle redo logs or PostgreSQL WAL; it only sees changes that already landed in a Snowflake table.

CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER_STREAM ON TABLE BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER;
SELECT * FROM BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER_STREAM;
Metadata columnMeaning
METADATA$ACTIONINSERT or DELETE
METADATA$ISUPDATETrue when the row is half of an update
METADATA$ROW_IDRow identifier for change tracking

A standard stream shows an update as a DELETE plus an INSERT with ISUPDATE set. Types: standard (inserts, updates, deletes), append-only (inserts), insert-only (some external-table cases). The stream's offset only moves forward when its rows are consumed in a committed DML statement, not when you SELECT from it. If nobody consumes it for longer than the retention window, it goes stale; watch for that with SHOW STREAMS.

Tasks

A task runs SQL on a schedule or a trigger.

CREATE OR REPLACE TASK BANK_DWH.CURATED.TASK_LOAD_CUSTOMER
  WAREHOUSE = WH_BANK_ETL
  SCHEDULE = '5 MINUTES'
  WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER_STREAM')
AS
  INSERT INTO BANK_DWH.CURATED.CUSTOMER_AUDIT (CUSTOMER_ID, CHANGE_ACTION, PROCESSED_AT)
  SELECT CUSTOMER_ID, METADATA$ACTION, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
  FROM BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER_STREAM;

ALTER TASK BANK_DWH.CURATED.TASK_LOAD_CUSTOMER RESUME;   -- tasks start suspended

Tasks can be chained into a dependency graph (load, validate, transform, refresh the mart), and newer releases also support triggered tasks. The WHEN check means the warehouse does not wake up when there is nothing to do.

A dynamic table is defined by a query. Snowflake keeps the result fresh to within a target lag you choose.

CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE BANK_DWH.CURATED.DT_BRANCH_DAILY
  TARGET_LAG = '10 minutes'
  WAREHOUSE = WH_BANK_ETL
  REFRESH_MODE = AUTO
AS
SELECT BRANCH_ID, TRANSACTION_DATE, SUM(AMOUNT) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, COUNT(*) AS TRANSACTION_COUNT
FROM BANK_DWH.RAW.TRANSACTIONS
GROUP BY BRANCH_ID, TRANSACTION_DATE;

Target lag is a freshness goal, not a guarantee. Refresh modes are AUTO, FULL and INCREMENTAL, and newer releases may add more, so confirm what your account supports.

Dynamic tablesStreams and tasks
You write the query, Snowflake plans the refreshYou write each step and the schedule
Dependencies are tracked for youYou design the orchestration
Good for SQL transformation pipelinesGood for MERGE, SCD2 and custom logic
Output is maintained automaticallyWrites to the target are explicit

My rule: use dynamic tables for plain transformation layers, and streams and tasks when the logic needs explicit MERGE, ordering or procedural code.

Part 3 · Modeling and transformation

Snowflake does not force a method. The choice comes from the sources, history and audit needs, and the reporting load; the Data modeling page covers that. A layout I use often is RAW (as received), STAGING (cleaned), CURATED (modeled) and MART (for reporting), with an AUDIT schema for control tables.

ApproachStructureGood for
KimballFacts and dimensionsReporting and BI
InmonIntegrated, usually 3NFEnterprise integration
Data VaultHubs, links, satellitesMany sources, full history
HybridVault or normalized core, dimensional martsLarge enterprises
CREATE TABLE BANK_DWH.MART.FACT_TRANSACTION (
  TRANSACTION_ID VARCHAR(50),
  CUSTOMER_SK    NUMBER,
  ACCOUNT_SK     NUMBER,
  BRANCH_SK      NUMBER,
  DATE_SK        NUMBER,
  AMOUNT         NUMBER(18,2));
-- grain: one row per transaction

State the grain before building. If a source event has several line items, the grain becomes one row per line, and the table changes with it.

Data Vault sketch

TableKey columns
HUB_CUSTOMERCustomer_HK, Customer_BK, Load_DTS, Record_Source
LINK_CUSTOMER_ACCOUNTCustomer_Account_HK, Customer_HK, Account_HK, Load_DTS
SAT_CUSTOMER_DETAILSCustomer_HK, Load_DTS, Customer_Name, City, HashDiff

Type 1 answers "what is the latest value?". Type 2 answers "what was the value on that date?". The Type 1 MERGE is the one on the SQL basics block. Type 2 needs two actions per changed customer: close the old row and add a new one.

Customer_SKCustomer_IDCityValid_FromValid_ToCurrent
1001C101Hyderabad2026-01-012026-11-16N
1002C101Mumbai2026-11-169999-12-31Y

A plain MERGE gives one action per source row, so the usual trick is to feed it each changed row twice: once with the real key (to close the old version) and once with a NULL key (so it falls into NOT MATCHED and inserts the new version).

MERGE INTO BANK_DWH.CURATED.DIM_CUSTOMER t
USING (
  SELECT s.CUSTOMER_ID AS MERGE_KEY, s.CUSTOMER_ID, s.CUSTOMER_NAME, s.CITY, s.UPDATED_AT
  FROM   BANK_DWH.STAGING.CUSTOMER_LATEST s
  UNION ALL
  SELECT NULL, s.CUSTOMER_ID, s.CUSTOMER_NAME, s.CITY, s.UPDATED_AT
  FROM   BANK_DWH.STAGING.CUSTOMER_LATEST s
  JOIN   BANK_DWH.CURATED.DIM_CUSTOMER d
    ON   d.CUSTOMER_ID = s.CUSTOMER_ID AND d.IS_CURRENT
  WHERE  d.CITY IS DISTINCT FROM s.CITY
) src
ON t.CUSTOMER_ID = src.MERGE_KEY AND t.IS_CURRENT
WHEN MATCHED AND t.CITY IS DISTINCT FROM src.CITY THEN
  UPDATE SET IS_CURRENT = FALSE, VALID_TO = src.UPDATED_AT
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (CUSTOMER_ID, CUSTOMER_NAME, CITY, VALID_FROM, VALID_TO, IS_CURRENT)
  VALUES (src.CUSTOMER_ID, src.CUSTOMER_NAME, src.CITY, src.UPDATED_AT, '9999-12-31', TRUE);

The staging table must hold one latest row per customer (use QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER(), shown below). A production pipeline also has to keep intervals from overlapping, process several changes for one key in order, and decide how deletes and late-arriving changes are handled.

ObjectStores its own data?Use
ViewNoReusable query
Secure viewNoHides definition, tighter exposure
Materialized viewYesSpeeds up supported repeated queries
Dynamic tableYesMaintained transformation result

Materialized views have restrictions on what the query may contain, and they cost credits to maintain. Use one when the same aggregate is queried over and over.

Ranking functions

BranchSalesROW_NUMBERRANKDENSE_RANK
A100111
B90222
C90322
D80443

ROW_NUMBER never repeats. RANK repeats on ties and leaves a gap. DENSE_RANK repeats on ties with no gap.

-- latest row per customer, a pattern I use constantly
SELECT *
FROM BANK_DWH.STAGING.CUSTOMER
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
          PARTITION BY CUSTOMER_ID
          ORDER BY UPDATED_AT DESC, INGEST_SEQUENCE DESC) = 1;

-- previous amount and running total
SELECT ACCOUNT_ID, TRANSACTION_DATE, AMOUNT,
       LAG(AMOUNT) OVER (PARTITION BY ACCOUNT_ID ORDER BY TRANSACTION_DATE, TRANSACTION_ID) AS PREVIOUS_AMOUNT,
       SUM(AMOUNT) OVER (PARTITION BY ACCOUNT_ID ORDER BY TRANSACTION_DATE, TRANSACTION_ID
                         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS RUNNING_TOTAL
FROM BANK_DWH.RAW.TRANSACTIONS;

QUALIFY filters on a window function, so you avoid wrapping the query in a subquery. It only helps if the ORDER BY has a reliable tie-breaker, which is what INGEST_SEQUENCE is for here.

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER_JSON (PAYLOAD VARIANT);
INSERT INTO BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER_JSON
SELECT PARSE_JSON('{"customer_id":101,"name":"Ravi","accounts":[{"id":"A1"},{"id":"A2"}]}');

SELECT PAYLOAD:customer_id::NUMBER AS CUSTOMER_ID,
       PAYLOAD:name::VARCHAR       AS CUSTOMER_NAME
FROM BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER_JSON;

SELECT c.PAYLOAD:customer_id::NUMBER AS CUSTOMER_ID,
       a.VALUE:id::VARCHAR           AS ACCOUNT_ID
FROM BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER_JSON c,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(INPUT => c.PAYLOAD:accounts) a;
Customer_IDAccount_ID
101A1
101A2

Use a colon to reach into the JSON, :: to cast to a type, and FLATTEN to turn an array into rows. Also handy: TRY_PARSE_JSON, OBJECT_CONSTRUCT, ARRAY_AGG, GET_PATH and TYPEOF. Cast early; leaving everything as VARIANT makes later queries slow and hard to read.

Part 4 · Protection, performance and cost

Time Travel lets you query or restore an earlier state of a table within its retention period (one day by default, longer on higher editions).

SELECT * FROM BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER AT (OFFSET => -3600);   -- one hour ago
UNDROP TABLE BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER;                          -- if still recoverable

CREATE TABLE BANK_DWH.STAGING.CUSTOMER_TEST CLONE BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER;
FeatureWhat it isWho uses it
Time TravelQueryable history inside the retention windowYou
Fail-safeA further recovery period for permanent tables, managed by SnowflakeSnowflake support only
Zero-copy cloneA logical copy that shares storage until data changesYou

A clone costs almost nothing at the start, then grows as either copy changes. It is the quickest way to give a developer a safe copy of production for testing. Longer Time Travel retention means more storage, so set it per table, not account-wide.

CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS BANK_ANALYST;
GRANT USAGE  ON DATABASE BANK_DWH TO ROLE BANK_ANALYST;
GRANT USAGE  ON SCHEMA   BANK_DWH.MART TO ROLE BANK_ANALYST;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES    IN SCHEMA BANK_DWH.MART TO ROLE BANK_ANALYST;
GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA BANK_DWH.MART TO ROLE BANK_ANALYST;

CREATE OR REPLACE MASKING POLICY BANK_DWH.CURATED.MASK_EMAIL AS (VAL STRING) RETURNS STRING ->
  CASE WHEN IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('PII_READER') THEN VAL ELSE '***MASKED***' END;
ALTER TABLE BANK_DWH.CURATED.DIM_CUSTOMER MODIFY COLUMN EMAIL
  SET MASKING POLICY BANK_DWH.CURATED.MASK_EMAIL;

CREATE OR REPLACE ROW ACCESS POLICY BANK_DWH.CURATED.REGION_POLICY AS (REGION VARCHAR) RETURNS BOOLEAN ->
  IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('BANK_ADMIN')
  OR (IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('NORTH_ANALYST') AND REGION = 'NORTH');

Grant to roles, never straight to users, and remember that future grants do not cover tables that already exist. Test a masking or row policy with a real analyst role before relying on it.

Beyond that: object tags and classification, access history, dependencies and lineage, data quality checks, secure data sharing, reader accounts, clean rooms, network policies, encryption and audit. The AWS page covers service accounts and key-pair login.

Open the Query Profile before changing anything. It shows where the time went, how much was scanned and whether data spilled to disk.

SymptomLook at
Large table scanPruning, clustering
Slow joinJoin keys, row multiplication, data skew
Spill to local or remote storageMemory: size up, or reduce the data in the step
Query waits in a queueConcurrency: another cluster or another warehouse
Slow aggregationCardinality, grouping
Same lookup over and overSearch Optimization
Same aggregate over and overMaterialized view or summary table
Long MERGEDuplicates in source, target pruning, write contention
High creditsRun time, serverless use, work that did not need to run
SELECT QUERY_ID, QUERY_TEXT, TOTAL_ELAPSED_TIME, EXECUTION_TIME, QUEUED_OVERLOAD_TIME,
       BYTES_SCANNED, BYTES_SPILLED_TO_LOCAL_STORAGE, BYTES_SPILLED_TO_REMOTE_STORAGE
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY
WHERE START_TIME >= DATEADD('day', -1, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
ORDER BY TOTAL_ELAPSED_TIME DESC
LIMIT 20;

Account Usage views need monitoring privileges and can lag by a while, so for something that just happened use the INFORMATION_SCHEMA functions.

Costs come from warehouse compute, serverless features, storage, data transfer and some extras. The easy part is warehouse arithmetic:

SizeHours per dayDays per monthClustersCredits per month
X-Small (1 credit/h)52211 × 5 × 22 × 1 = 110
Medium (4 credits/h)52214 × 5 × 22 × 1 = 440

This ignores the one-minute minimum on each start, newer warehouse generations that consume differently, storage and serverless. It is an estimate; billing is what counts.

CREATE OR REPLACE RESOURCE MONITOR BANK_WH_MONITOR
  WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = 1000 FREQUENCY = MONTHLY START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY
  TRIGGERS ON 80 PERCENT DO NOTIFY
           ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND;

A resource monitor covers warehouse credits only. Use budgets and account-level monitoring for the rest. The cheap wins, in the order I try them: short AUTO_SUSPEND, right-size each warehouse, one warehouse per workload, stop pointless refreshes, check large serverless features such as clustering and search optimization, and shorten Time Travel on big staging tables. A bigger warehouse is not always faster for loading, so test before assuming it.

Part 5 · Integration and practice

ProblemWhere to look
High target latencySnowflake apply queries, warehouse load, Replicate batch settings
MERGE misses a recordTarget row exists? Key mapping, CDC order, an earlier failure
Duplicate primary keysSource uniqueness, dedupe step, no enforcement on the target
Slow full loadFile sizes, parallelism, source read, COPY performance
Warehouse suspendedAuto-resume, permissions, endpoint settings
Queries queuedConcurrency, warehouse capacity
Wrong timestampsSource time zone, Snowflake timestamp type, session time zone
Data mismatchCDC position, deletes, filters, failed applies
SHOW WAREHOUSES;
SELECT QUERY_ID, QUERY_TEXT, EXECUTION_STATUS, TOTAL_ELAPSED_TIME, QUEUED_OVERLOAD_TIME
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY
WHERE START_TIME >= DATEADD('hour', -4, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
ORDER BY START_TIME DESC;

In an incident, line up the Snowflake query times against the Replicate task log and latency graph. Snowflake's own CDC (streams, dynamic tables) works on tables already loaded; an external tool like Replicate is what reads the source database's log. The Qlik Replicate page has the tuning side.

FeatureWhat it is for
External tablesQuery files in cloud storage in place
Iceberg tablesOpen table format
Hybrid tablesTransaction-style workloads with enforced keys
SnowparkPython, Java, Scala processing inside Snowflake
UDFs and stored proceduresReusable functions, multi-step logic
Cortex AI, vector dataAI functions and embeddings
Native AppsPackage and share applications
Secure data sharingShare data without copying files
Clean roomsJoint analysis of sensitive data
Replication and failoverBusiness continuity across regions or accounts
External functionsCall outside services
Network policiesLimit where logins can come from
Object tags, access historyClassification and audit
Query tagsAttribute cost to teams and pipelines
Schema evolutionAbsorb compatible new columns on load
CI/CDGit, Terraform, schemachange, deployment tests
QuestionAnswer
Why separate storage and compute?Independent scaling, workload isolation, and no copy of data per workload.
What is a micro-partition?The storage unit, around 50 to 500 MB uncompressed, with min/max metadata for pruning.
When do you increase warehouse size?When one query spills or is simply heavy.
When multi-cluster?When many concurrent queries queue.
Does Snowflake enforce primary keys?Not on standard tables. NOT NULL is enforced; hybrid tables enforce keys.
Streams versus Snowpipe?Snowpipe loads files in; a stream tracks changes already in a table.
Dynamic tables versus tasks?Declarative and managed, versus scripted and explicit.
Remove duplicates?QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() over the business key, ordered by update time and a sequence.
Time Travel versus Fail-safe?Time Travel is yours to query and restore; Fail-safe is Snowflake's last-resort recovery.
Why might a bigger warehouse not speed up loading?File count and size, source read speed or locks are the limit, not compute.
Implement SCD Type 2?Close the current row, insert the new row, keep intervals clean; use the double-feed MERGE.
Optimize a slow MERGE?Dedupe the source, make sure the target prunes on the join key, avoid concurrent writers.
What makes queries expensive?Full scans, spills, row multiplication in joins, long-running warehouses.
Design Customer 360?Grain and keys first, identity resolution, SCD2 customer dimension, fact tables per process, governance.
TermHook

WarehouseCompute that you start and stop

PruningSkip what cannot match
ClusteringKeep similar values together
Scale up / outBigger machine / more machines

When designing anything, I go in this order: business requirement, grain, ingestion, quality, transformation, history, security, performance, cost, monitoring, recovery.

Knowledge · CDC

Qlik Replicate

19 blocks on Qlik Replicate and Enterprise Manager: how CDC works, loading modes, fake CDC, tuning, internal parameters, Linux support and L3 troubleshooting. Tap a block to open it.

Part 1 · Basics and architecture

Qlik Replicate copies data from one system to another. It does that in two stages: a full load of what already exists, then CDC (change data capture), which follows new changes. In the setup these notes assume, the sources are Oracle (including ASM), SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL and RDS/Aurora, and the targets are Snowflake, Kafka, S3 and PostgreSQL, all run from Linux servers.

A bank example: account A101 goes from ₹50,000 to ₹55,000. The database commits the transaction, writes it to its log, Replicate reads it from that log, holds it briefly, and applies it to Snowflake or publishes it to Kafka. Nobody ran a query on the account table to find the change.

Full loadCDC
Copies rows that already existFollows changes as they happen
Heavy on source and target for a whileSteady, light read of the log
Used to initializeUsed to stay in sync
Can take hours for big tablesAims for seconds of latency

Replicate and Enterprise Manager are two different things

Qlik ReplicateEnterprise Manager
Runs the tasksManages the Replicate servers centrally
Reads source changes, applies to targetShows status, latency, errors
Keeps task stateStart and stop, access control, APIs
Runs on the replication hostCovers many registered servers

If Enterprise Manager is down, tasks keep running; you lose the central view, not the replication. What the UI and APIs offer depends on the versions installed.

Inside a task there are four stages. Capture reads the source log. The sorter holds changes until their transaction commits and puts them in commit order. Apply writes them to the target. State and recovery positions live in the task's repository (some of it in SQLite files) and in sorter storage on disk.

SourceWhere the changes come fromWhat to verify
OracleRedo and archived logs (LogMiner or the binary reader), ASM when usedARCHIVELOG mode, supplemental logging, access to redo and archive paths
SQL ServerTransaction log, via MS-Replication or MS-CDC depending on setupRecovery model, log backups, permissions
MySQLBinary loglog_bin on, binlog_format ROW, row image, retention
PostgreSQLLogical decoding and a replication slotwal_level, slots, WAL senders; on RDS the parameter group

These are not interchangeable. An Oracle SCN, a SQL Server LSN, a PostgreSQL LSN and a MySQL binlog position are all just a bookmark in a different book, which is why recovery steps differ per source.

Part 2 · Loading and applying changes

ModeWhat it doesUse it when
Full load onlyOne-time copyMigrations, static reference data
Full load + apply changesCopy, then keep the target in syncThe usual case for a mirror in Snowflake or a database
Apply changes onlyStarts from a log position or timestamp, no copyTarget already loaded, or recovery
Store changesWrites every change into change tables, with before and after images and metadataYou want history, audit or your own downstream merge
Log stream stagingOne task reads the source log, child tasks read from itMany tasks on the same source tables

Full load options

  • Parallel tables: how many tables load at once. More is not always faster; the source disks or the warehouse often become the limit.
  • Parallel load of one big table: split by partitions, ranges or segments so one huge table does not hold up the task.
  • If the target table exists: drop and create, truncate, or leave it. Pick this deliberately; truncate on the wrong task is a classic way to lose a table.
  • Reload a single table without touching the others, when only one table has gone wrong.

Batch versus transactional apply

Batch optimized applyTransactional apply
HowNets changes by key, loads them in bulk, runs one MERGE and DELETEReplays each source transaction in order, statement by statement
Speed on Snowflake, RedshiftFar faster, usually the only sensible choicePainfully slow at volume
LatencyRises with the batch intervalLow per transaction
Good forCloud warehouses, high volumeLow-volume OLTP targets where every transaction must keep its boundary
Watch forA bad row can push the batch into slower one-by-one handlingFalls behind quickly if the source is busy

Batch apply nets changes by key, so tables without a primary key or unique index behave badly on it. This is the first thing I check when a MERGE behaves oddly.

Real CDC reads the database's own log. "Fake" CDC (also called query-based or poll-based) has no access to the log, so it keeps asking the source what changed. It is used when there is no log to read: a SaaS API, Tally, a payment gateway, a read replica without log access, or a table owned by a vendor you cannot change.

TechniqueHow it worksCatch
Timestamp or watermark columnWHERE modified_at > last_runNeeds a reliable column, and someone must maintain it
Version or sequence columnPull rows with a higher ID or versionCatches inserts well, updates only if the version moves
Trigger-basedTriggers write changes into an audit tableAdds cost to every transaction on the source; DBAs often refuse
Snapshot compareCompare a full copy with the last one, using hashesReads the whole table every run
Scheduled full reloadReplace everything on a timerSimple, wasteful, and a gap while it runs

Advantages and disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Works where there is no log accessMisses deletes unless you add separate delete detection
No special source configuration or licencesMisses intermediate changes: A to B to C is seen only as C
Easy to build and understandPuts query load on the source, and every poll is a read
Fine for small tables and daily reportingLatency is the polling interval, not seconds
Portable across almost any sourceDepends on clocks and a trustworthy modified date; late commits slip through
Cheap to startNo commit ordering or transaction boundaries preserved

Making it safer

  • Re-read an overlap window (for example the last 10 to 15 minutes) and merge by key, so late commits are caught and reruns are harmless.
  • Keep the watermark in a separate control table, and move it only after the load succeeds.
  • Detect deletes with a key-only comparison against the source, or ask the owner for a soft-delete flag.
  • Reconcile counts and sums regularly, since this method fails quietly.
SELECT *
FROM   core.accounts
WHERE  modified_at >= :last_watermark - INTERVAL '15' MINUTE
  AND  modified_at <  :run_start;      -- fixed upper bound for repeatable runs

When I would accept it: small or slowly changing tables, sources with no log, reports that tolerate hours of delay, and anywhere deletes are rare or flagged. When I would not: payments, ledgers, anything audited, anything where a missed delete or a skipped intermediate state changes a number someone signs off.

Part 3 · Endpoints and administration

Oracle

  • Client libraries and credentials, supplemental logging, ARCHIVELOG mode.
  • Access to redo and archived logs; for ASM, the disk groups, credentials and paths.
  • A supported capture method, and enough archive retention to cover any outage.
SELECT LOG_MODE FROM V$DATABASE;
SELECT SUPPLEMENTAL_LOG_DATA_MIN FROM V$DATABASE;
SELECT CURRENT_SCN FROM V$DATABASE;

SQL Server

SELECT name, recovery_model_desc, log_reuse_wait_desc
FROM sys.databases;

A log_reuse_wait_desc of REPLICATION usually means the log is waiting on the capture process.

MySQL

SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_bin';
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'binlog_format';      -- want ROW
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'binlog_row_image';
SHOW MASTER STATUS;   -- newer versions: SHOW BINARY LOG STATUS

PostgreSQL

SHOW wal_level;                 -- logical
SHOW max_replication_slots;
SHOW max_wal_senders;
SELECT slot_name, active, restart_lsn, confirmed_flush_lsn
FROM pg_replication_slots;

An inactive slot makes PostgreSQL keep WAL forever, and the source disk fills up. On RDS or Aurora, extra parameter-group settings and privileges apply.

Error or signFirst place to look
ORA-15001ASM disk group not mounted or not reachable
ORA-16000Database opened read-only
Missing archived logRetention too short, or a gap after a backup job removed it
Redo read failurePermissions, capture setup, log availability

Snowflake

Account, authentication (key pair or OAuth where supported), warehouse, database and schema, a role with the right grants, network access and staging. Quick checks:

SELECT CURRENT_WAREHOUSE(), CURRENT_ROLE(), CURRENT_DATABASE(), CURRENT_SCHEMA();
SHOW WAREHOUSES;
SELECT QUERY_ID, QUERY_TEXT, EXECUTION_STATUS, TOTAL_ELAPSED_TIME
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.QUERY_HISTORY(
       DATEADD('hour', -1, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()))
ORDER BY START_TIME DESC;

Kafka / Confluent

Bootstrap servers, authentication, TLS, topic naming, serialization, Schema Registry, partitioning, producer settings and error handling. Ordering is guaranteed inside a partition, not across a topic. So choose the message key carefully, normally the source primary key, so all changes for account A101 land in the same partition and stay in order.

Amazon S3

Bucket, region, IAM role, prefix, file format, compression, encryption, file naming, and what picks the files up afterwards. Think about file size early: thousands of tiny files are a problem for whoever reads them later.

QuestionCommand
What server is this?hostname -f; cat /etc/os-release; uptime; timedatectl
Which Replicate processes are running?ps -ef | grep -Ei '[r]eplicate|[r]epagent|[a]ttunity'
What is eating memory?ps -eo pid,ppid,user,%cpu,%mem,rss,vsz,etime,cmd --sort=-rss | head -20
How much memory is really free?free -h; vmstat 1 5
Who is using swap?swapon --show, then read VmSwap from /proc/PID/status
Is the disk full?df -h; df -i
Where did it go?du -h --max-depth=1 /data | sort -hr | head -20
Large files?find /data -type f -size +1G -printf '%s %p\n' | sort -nr | head
df says full, du disagreessudo lsof +L1 (deleted files still held open)
Disk slow?iostat -xz 1 10
Network?ss -tanp; ss -lntp
Service state and logssystemctl status areplicate; journalctl -u areplicate -n 100 --no-pager
What has a file open?lsof -p PID; fuser -v path
Mounts and devicesfindmnt; lsblk -f

Two reminders. Linux "used" memory includes cache, so look at the available column and at swap activity, not just used. And df is free space on a filesystem while du is what a directory holds, which is the easiest way to remember them.

Do not run swapoff -a on a busy server with little free RAM, and never chmod -R 777 an installation.

The default install path on Linux is /opt/attunity/replicate, the service is usually areplicate, and the default REST port is 3552. Package names and options vary by release, so follow the guide for your exact build.

Install outline

  1. Check OS, kernel, CPU, RAM, disk, network paths, drivers, service account, TLS and firewall.
  2. Prepare storage for the data directory, sorter and backups, with correct ownership.
  3. Install the RPM (rpm -ivh), then verify with rpm -q areplicate and systemctl status areplicate.
  4. Configure license, drivers, data directory, sorter storage and management access.
  5. Create and test endpoints before any production task.

repctl

cd /opt/attunity/replicate/bin
source ./arep_login.sh
./repctl.sh help
./repctl.sh exportrepository                      # default data directory
./repctl.sh -d /data/replicate exportrepository   # custom data directory
./repctl.sh -d /data/replicate importrepository json_file=/secure/backup/Replication_Definition.json

Export is routine and worth scheduling. Import is a recovery operation under change control, because it can overwrite tasks and endpoints. Task start, stop and resume subcommands differ by release, so use the UI, Enterprise Manager or the documented API instead of guessing a command.

Upgrade checklist

BeforeAfter
Inventory instances, tasks, versions and driversInstances and task repositories load
Confirm the supported upgrade path (older builds may need a step in between)Endpoints connect, drivers work
Check source and target compatibilityCDC resumes without losing log position
Back up task definitions and data directoriesLatency returns to its normal level
Note task states and recovery positionsEnterprise Manager still matches
Confirm source log retention covers the outageNo new repeating errors in the logs
Test in UAT, agree the rollback planDo not resume every task blindly

An RPM upgrade can leave a repctl.cfg.rpmnew file when the configuration changed. Merge it by hand. For the latest releases, read Qlik's current release notes, since versions and upgrade paths change.

Part 4 · Tuning and performance

SettingControlsTrade-off
Tables loaded in parallelConcurrent full-load tablesSpeed against pressure on source, network and target
Batch apply intervalHow long changes are gathered before applyingFewer, bigger commits against higher latency
Memory limit for batchesSize at which a batch is forced outRAM against disk spill
Changes per statement or transactionMaximum rows in one applyThroughput against memory and recovery work
Transaction duration and memory (offload)When open transactions move from RAM to diskMemory against disk I/O
Error handlingRetry, stop, ignore, logAvailability against correctness
Table preparationDrop, truncate, leaveSafety against a clean start
Logging levelDetail written to logsDiagnostics against overhead and disk

Defaults I remember (check your build)

SettingTypical default
Tables loaded in parallel5
Transaction memory before offload1024 MB
Transaction duration before offload60 seconds
Batch interval, longer than / less than1 second / 30 seconds
Full load commit rate10,000 records

These are defaults from the documentation as I know it; names and ranges move between versions, so open the task settings on your build to confirm. Nothing here is a universal best value.

Parallelism example. Going from 4 to 8 parallel tables helps if the source and target have room. If the real limit is source disk I/O, the network or the warehouse, it makes things worse.

Internal parameters live in the endpoint under Advanced → Internal Parameters. They are not part of the normal UI because the defaults suit most cases. Treat them as tools for a specific, measured problem, preferably with Qlik support on the call.

Parameter or settingWhereWhat it influencesConfidence
readAheadBlocksOracle sourceHow many redo blocks are read per I/O. Larger values cut round trips on very busy redoDocumented
parallelASMReadThreadsOracle source with ASMThreads that read redo or archive blocks from ASMDocumented
asmUsePLSQLArrayOracle source with ASMReads ASM data through PL/SQL arrays, reducing round tripsDocumented
Logging components (SOURCE_CAPTURE, SORTER, TARGET_APPLY, PERFORMANCE and others)Task loggingRaise one component to Trace or Verbose briefly to see where time goesDocumented
Maximum file size, apply with MERGESnowflake targetSize of staged files, and set-based apply instead of row by rowDocumented in the endpoint
asmUseDBVersion, asmThreads, ociPrefetchRows, logFileReadBufferSize, cdcBatchSize, ignoreTxnRollback, lookupBufferSize, useDirectAsmAccess, skipAsmCheckAppear in some field notesVarious ASM and read-buffer behaviorsCould not confirm; ask Qlik support for the exact name and effect on your build

Rules I follow

  1. Find the bottleneck first. Do not tune blind.
  2. Change one parameter at a time and measure throughput and latency before and after.
  3. Record every internal parameter in the runbook and in the exported task JSON, because they are non-default and can surprise you at upgrade time.
  4. Retest after each version upgrade; a parameter can change meaning or be dropped.
  5. Do not copy a number from a blog. Ranges depend on redo volume, storage and RAM.
What you seeLikely stageLook at
Source latency high, target latency near zeroSource captureSlow redo or archive reads, ASM contention, network to the source, LOB lookups
Sorter folder growingSorter and memory spillLong open transactions, offload memory settings, target backlog
Source latency low, target latency climbingTarget applyWarehouse queueing, locks, missing primary keys, batch settings, apply errors
Both highShared causeNetwork, an overloaded Replicate host, a very large transaction
Throughput zero for hoursIdle source or stalled taskCompare source activity, task state and logs

The best single place to start is the task log with the PERFORMANCE component enabled, because it shows which stage is behind.

Throughput is not latency

If the source produces 50,000 changes a second and the target applies 40,000, the pipeline looks busy and healthy, yet the backlog grows by 10,000 a second. After a minute that is 600,000 changes waiting. A fast pipeline can still fall behind.

TermMeaning
ThroughputChanges per second
Source latencyHow far capture is behind the source
Target latencyHow far apply is behind capture
End-to-end latencySource commit to visible on target
BackpressureSlow downstream slowing the upstream
SpillMemory work written to disk
CheckpointSaved resume position
top -H            # CPU by thread
vmstat 1 10       # run queue, swap in/out
iostat -xz 1 10   # %util and await per device
df -h ; df -i     # space and inodes
ss -tanp          # connections
du -sh /data/sorter_storage/*

High %util can mean a saturated device, high await means requests are waiting, and a big throughput number alone proves nothing. Compare with the baseline for that server.

Scale up (a larger warehouse) when QUERY_HISTORY shows bytes spilled to local or remote storage during Replicate's MERGE statements, or when one huge batch, for example several million rows from a nightly ERP job, takes a long time to merge into a very large table. Doubling the size roughly doubles memory and cache, and a heavy MERGE often gets close to twice as fast, though not always.

Scale out (multi-cluster) when queries queue because many tasks share one warehouse and fire COPY and MERGE cycles together. Better still, give Replicate its own warehouse so BI and dbt queries never wait behind CDC, or the other way round.

Lock contention

Snowflake allows reads during a MERGE, but two writers on the same table block each other. Usual culprits: two Replicate tasks writing to one table, or a dbt model or stored procedure updating the Replicate target while a batch applies. Downstream jobs should read from that table, not modify it.

SHOW LOCKS IN ACCOUNT;
-- history of lock waits
SELECT * FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.LOCK_WAIT_HISTORY
ORDER BY REQUESTED_AT DESC LIMIT 50;

Batch tuning for cloud warehouses

Short batch intervals mean many small COPY and MERGE cycles, which cost credits and often run slower overall. Raising the "longer than" interval lets a meaningful micro-batch build up; the "less than" limit still forces an apply so the SLA holds. Large batches use more memory and make recovery slower. Try production-like volumes and compare sustained throughput, p95 latency, CPU, memory and credits before settling on numbers.

Before scaling anything up, look at the apply exceptions table. One bad row can push a batch into slow row-by-row handling, and no warehouse size fixes that.

Part 5 · Operations and recovery

The sorter holds changes until their transaction commits. If a source job updates ten million rows without an intermediate commit, Replicate keeps that transaction until the COMMIT arrives, and spills to disk once it passes the memory threshold. A stalled target has the same effect.

Why sorter storage grows

  • Target cannot apply fast enough, or is unreachable.
  • Large or long-running source transactions.
  • High incoming change rate and too little memory.
  • A recovery backlog after an outage.

Raising the transaction memory threshold (the default is 1024 MB) reduces disk churn if the server has RAM to spare. Lowering the duration threshold moves stale transactions to disk earlier. To find the culprit on the source:

-- Oracle
SELECT s.sid, s.serial#, t.start_time, t.used_ublk
FROM   v$transaction t JOIN v$session s ON s.taddr = t.addr
ORDER  BY t.start_time;
-- SQL Server
DBCC OPENTRAN;

An old open transaction holds back the low-watermark, so the DBA or application team has to commit or end it.

SQLite files and repository state

A task directory holds files such as dynamic_metadata.sqlite, deferred_target_apply_operations.sqlite, notifications.sqlite, a StateManager folder, a sorter folder and the task repo file. They are not logs. Symptoms of trouble are "database is locked", SQLITE_BUSY, a task that will not initialize or resume, or repeated crashes.

Investigate in this order: find the task processes, check what has the file open (lsof | grep dynamic_metadata.sqlite or fuser -v), then disk space and inodes, the filesystem under the task (findmnt -T), and finally the logs. Look for the first error before the lock message, not the last one.

Do not delete .sqlite or sorter files to clear a lock. They can hold the only valid resume position. Deleting them can break CDC resume, cause inconsistency or force a full reload of the task's tables. The safe order is: stop the task properly, confirm its process exited, capture logs and diagnostics, back up the whole task state, find the real cause, follow Qlik's version-specific recovery steps, and reconcile the target.

Stop, terminate, restart

ActionEffectRisk
Stop the task in the UI or Enterprise ManagerControlled shutdownLowest
kill -TERM on the correct task PIDAsks the process to clean upMedium
kill -KILLCannot be caught; state may be left uncleanHigh, last resort
Restart the serviceInterrupts every task on that instanceWidest

Never run pkill -9 -f replicate on a host with several tasks. Identify the exact PID first with ps -fp PID and pstree -ap PID.

  • Log stream staging. If four tasks read the same 20 Oracle tables, one staging task reads the redo once and the child tasks read from Replicate's local copy. The source sees one reader instead of four.
  • Supplemental logging. Primary-key supplemental logging produces less redo than logging all columns. Use all-column logging only when a target transformation really needs the before values.
  • Select only what is needed: fewer tables and columns, and filters, mean less to read, store and apply.
  • Keep archive retention long enough to survive an outage and a slow recovery.
  • Large LOBs: they cost extra lookups; use the LOB handling options that fit your size limits.

Mounts

lsblk -f ; findmnt ; df -Th
sudo mkdir -p /data/sorter_storage
sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /data/sorter_storage   # only if the device is the intended, already formatted one
sudo blkid /dev/sdb1
# /etc/fstab entry
UUID=<verified-uuid> /data/sorter_storage ext4 defaults,nofail 0 2
sudo mount -a

Never format a device or mount over a directory that already holds production data without confirming the device, filesystem and migration plan. Moving the sorter of an active task needs a controlled stop and a supported procedure, and a symbolic link must not be swapped in under a running task.

Cron

Format: minute hour day month weekday command. 0 2 * * * runs daily at 02:00 in the cron daemon's timezone. Cron is fine for archived logs, diagnostic exports and old backups. It must never delete active task folders, sorter files, SQLite files or checkpoints, because a file's age says nothing about whether it is still needed for recovery.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
ARCHIVE_DIR="/data/qlik_archived_logs"
LOG_FILE="/var/log/qlik_housekeeping.log"
RETENTION_DAYS=45

[[ -d "$ARCHIVE_DIR" ]] || { echo "Archive directory missing" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "Started: $(date -Is)" >> "$LOG_FILE"
# dry run first: only lists what would be deleted
find "$ARCHIVE_DIR" -xdev -type f -mtime +"$RETENTION_DAYS" -print >> "$LOG_FILE"
# enable after review:
# find "$ARCHIVE_DIR" -xdev -type f -mtime +"$RETENTION_DAYS" -delete
echo "Completed: $(date -Is)" >> "$LOG_FILE"

Install it with sudo install -m 750 under a restricted service account. Note that -mtime +7 counts whole 24-hour periods; for an exact 168 hours use -mmin +10080.

Part 6 · Troubleshooting and practice

SymptomLikely causeFirst check
database is locked / SQLITE_BUSYConcurrent access, stuck process, slow storageWho has the file open, filesystem health
Sorter memory threshold reachedTarget backlog or long transactionsTarget latency, sorter disk and memory
Source latency highCapture behindLog reader, source load, log availability
Target latency highSlow applyTarget queries, locks, staging, batch behavior
Zero throughputIdle source or stalled taskSource activity, task state, logs
SQL Server log errorsLog access or capture setupSQL Server log, prerequisites
Oracle ASM errorsDisk group or credentialsDisk groups, paths, credentials
PostgreSQL slot problemSlot inactive, WAL retention, permissionspg_replication_slots
MySQL TLS renegotiation errorDriver or TLS incompatibilityClient library, TLS settings, supported versions
Kafka topic errorTopic missing, ACL, connectivityTopic, brokers, permissions
Snowflake MERGE conflictMissing or mismatched row, duplicate keys, apply orderTarget keys, error handling policy
Snowflake timeoutHeavy query or warehouse pressureQuery history, locks, warehouse load
Service will not startConfig, permissions, libraries, portjournalctl, install state
Too many open filesDescriptor limitulimit and open descriptors

Example: latency jumps from 10 seconds to 45 minutes (Oracle to Snowflake)

  1. Source: is redo capture still advancing?
  2. Replicate: compare source and target latency.
  3. Sorter: backlog, memory, disk, long transactions.
  4. Snowflake: warehouse load, query history, locks, MERGE, staging.
  5. Network: throughput, retries, dropped connections.
  6. Fix the cause, then confirm the backlog is actually shrinking.

Increase the warehouse only if the evidence says compute is the limit. It will not help against a lock, a network problem, a single-threaded apply path, tiny batches or a capture problem.

A task showing Running does not mean CDC is healthy. Check that capture is advancing, apply is advancing, latency is normal and the data reconciles.

For each task, keep a baseline: normal latency, throughput, source log retention, sorter use, target apply behavior, recovery position and known error patterns. With a baseline, an incident is a comparison, not a guess.

CheckHow
Latency trendEnterprise Manager, task monitor
Capture progressPosition or timestamp moving in the log
Row counts and sumsScheduled reconciliation source against target
DiskSorter and data directory growth alerts
Source log retentionDays available against the longest likely outage
ErrorsApply exceptions table, task logs

Five rules

  1. Do not delete task state to fix a symptom without a supported recovery procedure.
  2. Do not restart the whole service for one failing task before checking the other tasks.
  3. Do not tune before finding the bottleneck, and measure before and after.
  4. Do not upgrade without a repository backup, a compatibility check and a rollback plan.
  5. Do not call CDC healthy because the status says Running.
QuestionAnswer
Full load versus CDC?Full load copies what exists; CDC follows changes from the log afterwards.
Replicate versus Enterprise Manager?Replicate runs tasks; Enterprise Manager manages and monitors servers and tasks.
Source latency is high and target latency is low. Where is the problem?In capture: log reads, ASM, network to the source.
Target latency is climbing?In apply: warehouse, locks, keys, batch settings, apply errors.
Why does the sorter fill up?Open or large transactions, a slow target or too little memory.
Can you delete the sorter folder?Not while the task may need it for recovery; it can force a reload.
What is fake CDC and when do you use it?Polling with a watermark or snapshot compare when the log is unavailable; it misses deletes and in-between changes.
Batch apply or transactional apply for Snowflake?Batch apply; transactional row by row does not scale on a cloud warehouse.
Do you add warehouse size when latency rises?Only if spill or queueing shows compute is the limit; check locks and apply errors first.
What do you record after using an internal parameter?Name, value, reason, date, in the runbook and the exported task JSON, and retest after upgrades.
TermMeaning or hook
Full loadCopy what exists
CDCFollow what changes
Fake CDCAsk the table instead of reading the log
SorterBuffer and order by commit
CheckpointWhere to resume
Source latencyHow far capture is behind
Target latencyHow far apply is behind capture
ThroughputChanges per second
BacklogIncoming minus applied
Batch optimized applyNet the changes, then MERGE
Store changesKeep every change as a row
Log streamRead the source log once
SCN / LSN / WAL / binlogOracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL log positions
Supplemental loggingExtra columns written to the Oracle redo

Semantic modeling

Ontology and knowledge graphs, in plain words

13 blocks: what an ontology is, how triples, OWL, SHACL and SPARQL fit together, how tables map into a graph, and a small sample you can click. Synthetic data only.

What you'll learn
  1. Foundations: why, triples, taxonomy vs ontology
  2. Languages and standards: OWL, SHACL, SPARQL
  3. Mapping and tools: R2RML, Stardog, GraphDB
  4. Try the working sample
  5. GenAI, pharma standards, governance
  6. Interview questions
Foundations

A normal data model answers questions you already know to ask. Tables, keys and joins are perfect for that. The trouble starts when the meaning of the data has to be shared by many teams and machines. One system says Drug, another says Product, a third says Medication. A fourth lists 'Humira' while the fifth lists 'adalimumab'. All of them are the same thing, and no foreign key will tell you so.

An ontology is a model that writes down the meaning in a form that both people and software can read: what things exist, how they are grouped, and how they connect. A knowledge graph is that model filled with real facts.

When a table model is enough, and when it is not

SituationPlain tablesOntology / graph
One team, fixed reportsBest choiceOverkill
Many sources use different words for one thingMapping tables grow foreverMap each source once to a shared concept
Questions like 'everything connected to this drug within 3 steps'Many self-joins, slow and hard to readA path query, one line
Rules like 'every biologic is a drug'Written again in every reportWritten once, applied everywhere
A machine (or LLM) must understand the dataColumn names onlyDefined terms it can look up

Analogy to remember: A table model is a filing cabinet. An ontology is the cabinet plus a dictionary that every clerk, and every computer, agrees on.

A fair note: A graph does not replace your warehouse. Most large companies keep facts in tables and use the graph as a meaning layer on top. Say this in an interview and you will sound practical, not fashionable.

RDF stores everything as short sentences of three parts, called triples: subject (the thing), predicate (the relationship) and object (the value or the other thing). That is all. A graph is just a pile of these sentences, where the end of one can be the start of another.

The same facts written as text (Turtle format)

@prefix ex: <http://example.org/pharma#> .

ex:Patient_P1  ex:enrolledIn  ex:Trial_T100 .
ex:Trial_T100  ex:studies     ex:Adalimumab .
ex:Adalimumab  ex:treats      ex:Psoriasis .
ex:Patient_P1  ex:birthDate   "1984-03-02" .

Three words you will hear

WordPlain meaningExample
URI / IRIA globally unique name for a thing, written like a web addresshttp://example.org/pharma#Adalimumab
LiteralA plain value such as text, number or date"1984-03-02"
Named graphA label that groups triples so you know where they came fromTriples loaded from the clinical system

Analogy to remember: A triple is a sentence with exactly three words: who, does what, to whom. Learn to read a graph by reading its arrows as sentences.

A fair note: Because every fact has the same three-part shape, adding a new kind of fact needs no ALTER TABLE. That is the real advantage. The cost is that you lose the strict structure a table gives you, which is why SHACL (block 5) exists.

People mix these words up, so here is the ladder. Each rung adds a little more meaning.

LevelWhat it holdsReal-life exampleStandard
Controlled listA fixed set of allowed valuesCountry codesPlain table
TaxonomyTerms in a parent and child treeDisease categories: Heart disease, then HypertensionSKOS (broader, narrower)
ThesaurusA taxonomy plus synonyms and related terms'Heart attack' = 'myocardial infarction'SKOS (altLabel, related)
OntologyClasses, properties and rules, so software can reasonEvery Biologic is a Drug; a trial studies at least one DrugOWL

Analogy to remember: A taxonomy is a family tree. A thesaurus adds nicknames. An ontology adds the family rules, such as who may marry whom, that a computer can check.

SKOS is the light standard for taxonomies and thesauri. It has just a handful of words: prefLabel (the official name), altLabel (a synonym), broader and narrower (parent and child), related, and ConceptScheme (the whole vocabulary). Medical code lists such as MedDRA are usually published or modeled this way.

A fair note: Do not build an ontology when a SKOS list will do. Many reference data projects only need preferred names, synonyms and a hierarchy. Heavy OWL reasoning is a cost you take on only when someone actually needs the reasoning.

Languages and standards

OWL is the language for writing the rules of meaning. You can think of it as the logical model of the graph world. It has four building blocks.

BlockPlain meaningTable-world twinExample
ClassA kind of thingEntity / tableDrug, Trial, Patient
IndividualOne real thingA rowAdalimumab, Trial T100
Object propertyLinks two thingsForeign keyenrolledIn, studies
Data propertyLinks a thing to a valueColumnbirthDate, dose_mg
Subclass'is a kind of'Supertype / subtypeBiologic is a Drug

A tiny ontology in Turtle

ex:Drug        a owl:Class .
ex:Biologic    a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf ex:Drug .
ex:Trial       a owl:Class .

ex:studies     a owl:ObjectProperty ;
               rdfs:domain ex:Trial ;     # the subject must be a Trial
               rdfs:range  ex:Drug .      # the object must be a Drug

ex:birthDate   a owl:DatatypeProperty ;
               rdfs:domain ex:Patient ;
               rdfs:range  xsd:date .

Domain and range are the part people find odd at first. They are not validation rules. If you say ex:studies has range ex:Drug and someone writes a triple that studies 'Aspirin', the system does not complain. It concludes that Aspirin is a Drug. That is reasoning in action.

Analogy to remember: OWL is the label on the shelf, not the guard at the door. It says what things are. The guard is SHACL, next block.

A fair note: OWL works on an open-world assumption: if a fact is missing, the system does not assume it is false, only unknown. This is the opposite of how a database behaves, and it surprises almost everyone coming from SQL.

OWL describes meaning. SHACL checks quality. You write a shape, which says what a valid record must look like, and the engine reports every record that breaks it. It is the closest thing to NOT NULL, CHECK and foreign key constraints in the graph world.

ex:PatientShape a sh:NodeShape ;
  sh:targetClass ex:Patient ;
  sh:property [
    sh:path ex:birthDate ;
    sh:minCount 1 ;            # a birth date is required
    sh:datatype xsd:date ;
    sh:message "Patient needs a birth date" ] ;
  sh:property [
    sh:path ex:enrolledIn ;
    sh:class ex:Trial ;        # must point to a Trial
    sh:minCount 1 ] .
SQL constraintSHACL twin
NOT NULLsh:minCount 1
Data typesh:datatype
Foreign key to a tablesh:class
CHECK (value in list)sh:in (...)
Allowed length or patternsh:maxLength, sh:pattern

Analogy to remember: OWL tells you a car has four wheels. SHACL stands at the gate and refuses the car that arrives with three.

A fair note: SHACL is the answer to the common complaint that graphs are messy. In an interview, say: ontology for meaning, shapes for quality, and both are versioned like code.

SPARQL is SQL's cousin. Instead of choosing tables, you describe a pattern of triples with blanks (variables start with ?), and the engine finds everything that fits the pattern. Joins disappear, because shared variable names do the joining.

Question: which patients are in a trial of a biologic?

SQLSPARQL
SELECT p.patient_id
FROM patient p
JOIN enrollment e ON e.patient_id=p.patient_id
JOIN trial t ON t.trial_id=e.trial_id
JOIN drug d ON d.drug_id=t.drug_id
WHERE d.drug_class='Biologic';
SELECT ?p WHERE {
  ?p ex:enrolledIn ?t .
  ?t ex:studies    ?d .
  ?d a             ex:Biologic .
}
SQL ideaSPARQL idea
SELECT columnsSELECT ?variables
JOIN ... ONReuse the same ?variable in two patterns
WHEREPatterns inside { }
GROUP BY, COUNTGROUP BY, COUNT (same)
LEFT JOINOPTIONAL { ... }
Recursive CTEProperty path, such as ex:partOf+

Where SPARQL wins: walking relationships

# Every condition that sits anywhere under 'Nervous system disorder'
SELECT ?c WHERE { ?c rdfs:subClassOf+ ex:NervousSystemDisorder }

The + means 'one or more steps'. In SQL this needs a recursive CTE. Here it is a single character.

Analogy to remember: SQL asks 'which rows, joined how?'. SPARQL says 'find me anything shaped like this sketch'.

A fair note: For plain reporting, SQL is still faster to write and better supported. Use SPARQL where relationships and meaning are the point.

Mapping and tools

Your company already has data in relational tables. Copying all of it into a graph store is slow and creates a second version of the truth. R2RML is a mapping language that says 'this table becomes this class, this column becomes this property'. A tool such as Stardog can then answer graph questions by translating them to SQL on the live source. This is called a virtual graph.

<#TrialMap> a rr:TriplesMap ;
  rr:logicalTable [ rr:tableName "TRIAL" ] ;
  rr:subjectMap [ rr:template "http://example.org/pharma#Trial_{TRIAL_ID}" ;
                  rr:class ex:Trial ] ;
  rr:predicateObjectMap [
    rr:predicate ex:studies ;
    rr:objectMap [ rr:template "http://example.org/pharma#Drug_{DRUG_ID}" ] ] .
ApproachHow it worksGood whenWatch out for
Virtual graphQuery is rewritten to SQL at run timeData changes often, copying is not allowedSpeed depends on the source database
Materialized graphTriples are loaded into the graph storeHeavy graph analytics, reasoning at scaleA second copy to refresh and govern

Analogy to remember: R2RML is a bilingual dictionary taped to the table. You keep speaking SQL downstairs; upstairs, everyone speaks graph.

A fair note: Mapping is where most of the real work sits. The tool is the easy part; agreeing what each column really means is the hard part, and it is the same skill you use in source-to-target mapping.

These names appear in job descriptions all the time, and they are not competitors in every way. Some are for designing ontologies, others for storing and querying graphs, others for governing vocabularies.

ToolMain jobOne-line picture
ProtégéFree desktop editor for designing OWL ontologiesThe drawing board
TopBraid Composer / EDGAuthoring and governing ontologies, taxonomies and reference data, with workflowsThe drawing board plus an approval desk
StardogEnterprise knowledge graph platform with virtual graphs, reasoning and validationThe window onto your databases
GraphDB (Ontotext)Triple store with strong RDF and reasoning supportThe warehouse for triples
MarkLogicMulti-model store that can hold documents and triplesA filing room that also holds graphs
CenTree and similarVocabulary management for reference dataThe dictionary office

Analogy to remember: Editor to write the book, library to hold the books, librarian to approve new editions.

A fair note: Be straight about hands-on depth. If you have not run Stardog in production, say you understand how it works and have prepared with sample mappings and queries. That honesty goes down better than a bluff that falls apart at the first follow-up.

Hands-on sample

Below is a small synthetic pharma graph (made-up patients, trials and drugs). Pick a question, see the SPARQL, and see the answer. Then turn reasoning on and off and watch what changes.

SPARQL
Answer
All facts in the graph ( triples)
What to notice:
  • Run List every Drug with reasoning off. You get nothing, because nobody wrote that Adalimumab is a Drug. Turn reasoning on and both drugs appear, because a Biologic is a kind of Drug.
  • Run Nervous system conditions. The headache is found only through the hierarchy, which is the same trick that makes MedDRA-style hierarchies useful.
  • Run the SHACL check. It finds the patient with no birth date, which is the graph version of a NOT NULL test.
A fair note: This is a teaching toy that runs a small matcher in your browser, not a real SPARQL engine. The patterns and the results behave the way they would in Stardog or GraphDB on this tiny data.
Applying it
A language model writes fluent answers but does not know your company's facts, and it can invent. A knowledge graph holds exact, checkable facts. Putting the two together makes answers more reliable. The pairing is usually called GraphRAG.
Plain RAG (document search)GraphRAG
Finds text passages that look similar to the questionFollows relationships between defined things
Good for 'what does this document say?'Good for 'how is A linked to B through C?'
Can miss connections spread across documentsConnections are explicit and traceable
An ontology helps the LLM too: defined terms and synonyms reduce confusion, and the SHACL shapes keep the facts clean before the model ever sees them.
Analogy to remember: The LLM is a good talker. The graph is the fact-checker sitting next to it.
A fair note: It adds real cost: someone must build and maintain the graph. For a small document set, plain RAG is usually enough.
In pharma, the words are regulated. Different bodies publish standard vocabularies, and ontologies are a natural way to connect them.
StandardWhat it coversEveryday pictureTypical use
CDISC (SDTM, ADaM, CDASH)How clinical trial data is structured and submittedStandard forms for trial resultsSubmissions to regulators
MedDRAMedical terms for adverse events and conditions, in a five-level hierarchyOne dictionary for 'what went wrong'Safety reporting
IDMPStandard identification of medicinal productsA passport number for each medicineProduct data across regions
SNOMED CT / ICDClinical terms and disease codesClinical and billing dictionariesHealth records, coding
Why this suits a graph: the hierarchy is a ladder of 'broader' links (SKOS), versions are published twice a year, and queries like 'all events under nervous system disorders' are exactly the property-path trick from block 6.
Analogy to remember: MedDRA is a funnel. Start at the wide mouth (body system) and walk down to the exact term a patient reported.
A fair note: Exact term counts, level names and update schedules come from the publishers. Check the current release notes before quoting a number in an interview.
A vocabulary is shared by many systems, so changing it carelessly breaks reports and submissions. Governance is the set of habits that prevent that.
HabitWhat it meansEveryday picture
Owner and stewardA named person approves changes to each vocabularyThe editor of the dictionary
VersioningEvery release has a number and a date; old versions stay availableDictionary editions
Change workflowRequest, review, approve, publishA form with signatures
Deprecate, do not deleteRetire a term but keep it so old data still makes sense'Do not use' stamp, not the shredder
Mapping between versionsShow how old terms map to new onesA conversion chart
Quality gatesSHACL checks run before a release goes outA proofreader before printing
Analogy to remember: Treat vocabulary like software: pull request, review, tests, release notes.
A fair note: Tools such as TopBraid EDG give you this workflow out of the box, but the habits matter more than the tool. A spreadsheet with an owner and a version column beats an expensive tool nobody follows.
Interview
QuestionShort answer
What is the difference between a taxonomy and an ontology?A taxonomy is a tree of terms. An ontology adds classes, relationships and rules, so software can reason over the data.
Why not just use relational tables?Tables are great for known questions. A graph is better when meaning is shared across many sources, or when you need to walk relationships.
What do OWL and SHACL each do?OWL states what things mean and lets a reasoner infer more. SHACL checks that data meets a required shape.
What is open-world assumption?If a fact is missing, the system treats it as unknown, not false. SQL treats missing as false.
What is a virtual graph?A graph view over existing tables, defined with a mapping such as R2RML, so nothing is copied.
How would you start an ontology project?Pick one business question, list the concepts and terms, reuse a standard where one exists, build a small model, test with real queries, then grow it.
How do ontologies relate to a semantic layer?Both give business meaning to data. A semantic layer defines metrics and dimensions for BI; an ontology defines concepts and rules and can feed it.
How do you keep a vocabulary from drifting?Owners, versions, a change workflow, deprecation instead of deletion, and automated checks before release.
Where do knowledge graphs help GenAI?They supply exact facts and defined terms, so answers are grounded and traceable.
Have you built one in production?Answer honestly. Describe what you have done, such as data modeling, glossaries, mappings and lineage, and what you have prepared with samples.
Analogy to remember: Say the picture first (cabinet and dictionary), then the term (ontology), then one real example.


Quick notes
AWS, explained in plain words
16 blocks. Start with S3, IAM and Redshift basics, each with a diagram and an everyday picture, then move on to loading files from S3 into Snowflake and running the platform.
What you'll learn
  1. Start here · S3, IAM and Redshift basics
  2. S3 to Snowflake · Architecture and setup
  3. S3 to Snowflake · Loading files
  4. S3 to Snowflake · Administration and operations
Start here · S3, IAM and Redshift basics
Think of S3 as a huge storage building. You rent a bucket (one big locker room with a globally unique name) and put objects (files) in it. Each object is found by its key, which is just its full name. The slashes look like folders, but they are only part of the name. Analysts call the first part of the key a prefix.
Storage classes: how often do you open the box?
ClassUse it forPicture
StandardData read oftenFront desk drawer
Standard-IA (infrequent access)Read about monthlyCupboard in the next room
Glacier Instant / FlexibleArchives, rarely readBasement archive
Intelligent-TieringUnknown patternA clerk who moves boxes for you
Settings worth knowing on day one
SettingWhat it doesReal-life example
Block Public AccessStops the bucket from ever being open to the internetAlways on for bank data
VersioningKeeps old copies when a file is overwrittenRecover a bad file replaced by mistake
Lifecycle ruleMoves or deletes files by ageRaw files to Glacier after 90 days
Encryption (SSE-S3 or KMS)Scrambles data at restKMS key for customer files
Event notificationTells another service a file arrivedNew file triggers a load
A flow you will see everywhere
Partner uploads file→S3 bucket→Event notification→Queue or Lambda→Load into warehouse
Analogy to remember: A bucket is a locker room, an object is a file in a locker, the key is the locker label. Slashes are just part of the label.
A fair note: S3 is excellent for files but it is not a database. It has no rows, joins or updates in place. Name your prefixes by date and source from day one, because renaming millions of objects later means copying them.
IAM is the security guard of AWS. Each request is checked against one sentence: this principal may take this action on this resource.
PiecePlain meaningExample
UserA person's own loginAn analyst, with MFA turned on
GroupA set of users sharing accessfinance-analysts
RoleA badge anyone or anything can borrow for a whileA load job that reads S3
PolicyThe list of allowed (or denied) actionsRead the raw/customer/ prefix only
What a policy looks like
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket"],
    "Resource": [
      "arn:aws:s3:::bank-data-lake",
      "arn:aws:s3:::bank-data-lake/raw/customer/*"
    ]
  }]
}
This lets the holder list the bucket and read files under one prefix, and nothing else. If an action is not allowed, it is denied. An explicit deny always wins.


Trust policy versus permissions policy


A role has two parts. The trust policy says who may borrow the badge. The permissions policy says what the badge opens. Many "access denied" problems are a missing trust, not a missing permission.


When you get AccessDenied, check in this order
  1. Is the right principal making the call (check the role actually in use)?
  2. Does a policy allow the action on that exact resource?
  3. Is there an explicit deny somewhere?
  4. If the data is encrypted with KMS, may the principal use the key?
  5. Does the bucket policy also allow it?
Analogy to remember: Principal plus action plus resource. A role is a borrowed badge, and the trust policy decides who may borrow it.
A fair note: Wildcards like s3:* on all resources are fast to write and hard to defend in an audit. Start narrow and widen only when something genuinely needs it. Prefer roles with temporary keys over long-lived access keys.
Redshift is AWS's data warehouse. You write SQL and it answers, but under the hood the work is split across many machines. A leader node receives your query and makes a plan. Compute nodes each hold a share of the data and work at the same time. Each node is divided into slices, the smallest workers.
Why it is fast: columns and parallel work


Data is stored by column, so a query reading two columns of a twenty-column table touches only those two. Many slices work together, so the speed of a query depends on how evenly the data is spread.


The three table settings
SettingQuestion it answersPlain picture
Distribution styleWhich node holds which row?Dealing cards to players
Sort keyIn what order are rows stored on disk?Books on a shelf in date order
Compression encodingHow small can each column be packed?Vacuum-packing the box
Distribution styleHow it dealsUse it for
KEYSame key value goes to the same nodeLarge fact tables joined on that key
ALLA full copy on every nodeSmall dimension tables
EVENRound robinTables with no clear join key
AUTORedshift chooses and adjustsA safe default to start with
Two big tables joined on the same key and stored by that key stay on the same node, so the join needs no shuffling. That is the main reason to choose KEY.


A table and a load
CREATE TABLE fact_transaction (
  transaction_id  VARCHAR(30),
  account_id      VARCHAR(20),
  transaction_dt  DATE,
  amount          DECIMAL(18,2)
)
DISTKEY (account_id)
SORTKEY (transaction_dt);

COPY fact_transaction
FROM 's3://bank-data-lake/curated/transactions/'
IAM_ROLE 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/redshift-load'
FORMAT AS PARQUET;
Everyday upkeep
TaskWhy
ANALYZERefreshes statistics so the planner makes good choices
VACUUMReclaims space and re-sorts after many deletes or updates
Workload managementKeeps a heavy report from slowing the dashboards
Two ways to run it
OptionHow it worksPick it when
Provisioned clusterYou choose node type and countSteady, predictable workloads
ServerlessRedshift scales capacity for youSpiky or unpredictable use
Analogy to remember: Leader plans, compute nodes work, slices do the labor. Distribution is dealing cards, sort key is the shelf order.
A fair note: Redshift, Snowflake and BigQuery all solve the same problem with different knobs. Redshift gives you more control over distribution and sorting, which rewards careful design but also needs more tuning. Newer features such as AUTO settings and Serverless remove some of that work. Pick by workload, skills and where your data already lives.
S3 to Snowflake · Architecture and setup
Producers (Oracle CDC, SQL Server, Qlik Replicate, Python jobs, applications) drop files into an S3 landing bucket. From there data reaches Snowflake by one of two routes. Batch: an external stage points at the S3 path and a COPY INTO loads the files on a schedule. Event driven: S3 sends a notification to SQS and Snowpipe loads each file as it lands. Both end in a raw table; the rest of the pipeline is the same.


One rule I keep: COPY's load history stops the same file loading twice, but it is not deduplication. Rows still need to be deduplicated by business key, and loads still need to be repeatable without side effects.
ScenarioApproach
One CSV, onceExternal stage and COPY INTO
Several CSV filesCOPY INTO with a path or PATTERN
Daily filesDate-partitioned S3 prefixes and a scheduled COPY
Hourly filesScheduled COPY, or Snowpipe
Files arrive at unpredictable timesSnowpipe auto-ingest
Large historical backfillParallel batch COPY, many mid-sized files
Nested JSONVARIANT and FLATTEN
ParquetCOPY INTO with column matching
GZIP CSVCOPY with compression set or AUTO
A file is re-uploaded after a fixNew immutable file name, or a controlled reload
The same file is delivered twiceLoad metadata, plus dedupe by key
Bad recordsValidate, quarantine, retry
Schema changesAn explicit contract, or controlled schema evolution
One feed, several targetsLand raw once, transform downstream
CDC files from Qlik ReplicateOrdered processing using the operation and sequence columns
1. Bucket and layout
aws s3 mb s3://bank-data-lake-example --region ap-south-1
The name must be globally unique; this one is an example. In production: block public access, encryption, versioning where it helps, lifecycle rules, access logging and tight IAM permissions. A layout that works well:
s3://bank-data-lake-example/
  landing/customers/year=2026/month=11/day=16/customers_001.csv
  landing/transactions/year=2026/month=11/day=16/hour=10/transactions_001.csv
  landing/accounts/accounts_001.parquet
  archive/
  quarantine/
2. IAM policy (read only)
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::bank-data-lake-example/landing/*"] },
    { "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:ListBucket", "s3:GetBucketLocation"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::bank-data-lake-example",
      "Condition": { "StringLike": { "s3:prefix": ["landing/*", "landing/"] } } }
  ]
}
If the bucket uses a customer-managed KMS key, the role also needs permission to use that key.


3. Storage integration in Snowflake
CREATE OR REPLACE STORAGE INTEGRATION BANK_S3_INT
  TYPE = EXTERNAL_STAGE
  STORAGE_PROVIDER = 'S3'
  ENABLED = TRUE
  STORAGE_AWS_ROLE_ARN = 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/snowflake-s3-read-role'
  STORAGE_ALLOWED_LOCATIONS = ('s3://bank-data-lake-example/landing/');
This uses an IAM role, so no long-lived AWS keys sit inside the stage.


4. Read Snowflake's trust details
DESC INTEGRATION BANK_S3_INT;
Copy STORAGE_AWS_IAM_USER_ARN and STORAGE_AWS_EXTERNAL_ID exactly.


5. Trust policy on the AWS role
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": { "AWS": "<SNOWFLAKE_IAM_USER_ARN>" },
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
    "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "sts:ExternalId": "<SNOWFLAKE_EXTERNAL_ID>" } }
  }]
}
6. Stage and check
CREATE OR REPLACE STAGE BANK_DWH.RAW.STG_CUSTOMERS_S3
  URL = 's3://bank-data-lake-example/landing/customers/'
  STORAGE_INTEGRATION = BANK_S3_INT
  FILE_FORMAT = BANK_DWH.RAW.FF_CUSTOMER_CSV;     -- the file format must exist first

LIST @BANK_DWH.RAW.STG_CUSTOMERS_S3;
If LIST fails, check in order: the trust policy and external ID, bucket and prefix permissions, KMS access, the integration's allowed locations, and which Snowflake role is active.
S3 to Snowflake · Loading files
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER_RAW (
  CUSTOMER_ID VARCHAR(30), CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR(100), CITY VARCHAR(100),
  UPDATED_AT TIMESTAMP_NTZ,
  SOURCE_FILE VARCHAR(500), FILE_ROW_NUMBER NUMBER, LOADED_AT TIMESTAMP_LTZ);

CREATE OR REPLACE FILE FORMAT BANK_DWH.RAW.FF_CUSTOMER_CSV
  TYPE = CSV FIELD_DELIMITER = ',' SKIP_HEADER = 1
  FIELD_OPTIONALLY_ENCLOSED_BY = '"' TRIM_SPACE = TRUE
  EMPTY_FIELD_AS_NULL = TRUE NULL_IF = ('NULL','')
  TIMESTAMP_FORMAT = 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS' COMPRESSION = AUTO;
File format settingWhy it matters
SKIP_HEADER / PARSE_HEADERIgnore header rows, or read names from them (not both)
FIELD_DELIMITER, RECORD_DELIMITERComma, pipe, tab; row separator
FIELD_OPTIONALLY_ENCLOSED_BYQuoted fields that contain the delimiter
NULL_IF, EMPTY_FIELD_AS_NULLWhat counts as NULL
TRIM_SPACEStrip surrounding spaces
ENCODING, COMPRESSIONCharacter set, GZIP and others
ERROR_ON_COLUMN_COUNT_MISMATCHCatch rows with the wrong number of fields
Load with source metadata
Keeping the file name and row number on every row makes duplicate deliveries and bad rows far easier to trace.
COPY INTO BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER_RAW
FROM (
  SELECT t.$1::VARCHAR, t.$2::VARCHAR, t.$3::VARCHAR,
         TRY_TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(t.$4),
         METADATA$FILENAME, METADATA$FILE_ROW_NUMBER, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
  FROM @BANK_DWH.RAW.STG_CUSTOMERS_S3 t)
FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = BANK_DWH.RAW.FF_CUSTOMER_CSV)
ON_ERROR = 'ABORT_STATEMENT';
Add FILES = ('year=2026/month=11/day=16/customers_001.csv') for one file, PATTERN = '.*[.]csv' for a folder (adjust for .csv.gz), or point the stage path at a day's folder (@stage/year=2026/month=11/day=16/) for a daily load. For scheduled loads, calculate that path in the orchestrator or a stored procedure.


When column order changes
Positional loading ($1, $2) silently puts values in the wrong column if the source reorders them. Matching by header name avoids that:
CREATE FILE FORMAT BANK_DWH.RAW.FF_HEADER_CSV TYPE = CSV PARSE_HEADER = TRUE FIELD_OPTIONALLY_ENCLOSED_BY = '"';

COPY INTO BANK_DWH.RAW.CUSTOMER_SOURCE
FROM @BANK_DWH.RAW.STG_CUSTOMERS_S3
FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = BANK_DWH.RAW.FF_HEADER_CSV)
MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME = CASE_INSENSITIVE;
